items.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.title: Rethinking English Education In The Era Of Generative Ai And Global Englishes

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.venue: International Journal of Arts, Humanities & Social Science
items.abstract_text: The advent of generative AI has provoked an ontological crisis in language education, tempting policymakers to equate machine-generated output with human interpretive capacity. This article challenges the premise that such technologies render language learning obsolete, arguing instead that an AI-saturated landscape makes robust humanistic engagement more vital than ever. Addressing the “scholar’s dilemma,” the paper proposes a structural shift in higher education from traditional silos toward horizontal, cross-disciplinary integration. Because English functions as a global lingua franca (ELF) and exerts an algorithmic hegemony over large language models (LLMs), advanced proficiency remains indispensable for critically querying these platforms. We advocate for a pedagogical evolution from the mechanical transmission of referential information (informing) to facilitating imaginative exploration (engaging). Central to this shift is the reclamation of “literature with a small l” as the primary representational material used to cultivate students’ “textual power.” By prioritizing the interpretive struggle over cognitive offloading—a tension described here as the “Picasso Paradox”—educators can formalize a “fifth skill” (complex critical thinking in English). This framework provides the cognitive foundation for students to navigate an AI-saturated world not as passive users, but as active curators equipped with ethical discernment and epistemic agency.

items.title: Teacher Metacognitive Scaffolding, Productive and Substitutive Generative AI Offloading, and Self-Regulated Learning in Madrasah Aliyah

publication_date_provenance.reason: ProviderDeferred

items.abstract_text: Secondary school students increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), and evidence shows it can either support or weaken their self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether teacher metacognitive scaffolding (TMS) and AI literacy (AIL) are related to SRL through productive cognitive offloading (PCO) and substitutive cognitive offloading (SCO), and whether peer collaborative AI use (PCAU) strengthens the link between scaffolding and productive offloading. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 327 students from 24 classes in eight Indonesian madrasah aliyah (Islamic senior high schools) selected through stratified multistage cluster sampling. We analysed the data using partial least squares structural equation modelling with 10,000 bootstrap subsamples. The measurement model met the reliability and validity criteria. TMS was positively related to PCO (β = 0.378) and negatively related to SCO (β = −0.351), and AIL showed the same pattern with smaller coefficients. PCO was positively related to SRL (β = 0.291), whereas SCO was negatively related to it (β = −0.266). Both forms of offloading partially mediated the relationships of TMS and AIL with SRL. PCAU strengthened the TMS–PCO path (β = 0.257), and scaffolding was not significantly related to productive offloading when peer collaboration was low. The model explained 45.8% of the variance in SRL. The findings indicate that teacher guidance is associated with SRL both directly and, for nearly half of its total effect, through the way students offload their thinking to GenAI, particularly when students verify AI outputs together.

items.title: Too good to resist? Affective engagement and a competence–regulation gap predict self-reported over-reliance on generative AI among vocational foreign-language learners

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors ( n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out ( β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment ( β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own ( r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially ( r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance ( β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance ( M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

items.title: Survey of the impacts of generative artificial intelligence on critical thinking development in education

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative AI (GenAI) has been adopted across education faster than its effects on learning have been examined. Critical thinking is among the competencies most consistently demanded of graduates, and whether GenAI use strengthens or weakens it remains unsettled. This review examines how critical thinking is conceptualized and assessed in GenAI-mediated education, what impact GenAI has on students’ critical thinking, and how educators can integrate these tools to support its development. We searched Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, and the ACM Digital Library for records on GenAI and education published through June 2026, with no date limit on the conceptual and assessment literature for critical thinking.​ Supplementary background and pedagogical sources also included institutional reports, assessment resources, books, and educational websites. Records were screened in three stages by title, by abstract and conclusion, and by full text, yielding 66 studies for synthesis. GenAI has no uniform effect on critical thinking. Unstructured use is associated with reduced critical thinking enaction, cognitive offloading, and weakened metacognitive monitoring, while use that requires students to interrogate model output is associated with gains, most consistently in analysis and evaluation. The same models produce both outcomes, indicating that the determining variable is the demand the task places on the student. The configurations that produce gains each make reasoning a condition of task progress. Assessment has not kept pace, since instruments that score the submitted artefact cannot separate student reasoning from model contribution. We propose an 18-item self-report instrument that relocates measurement to the process of engaging with AI across all six dimensions of critical thinking. Whether GenAI strengthens or substitutes for student reasoning depends on task and assessment design rather than on the tools themselves.

items.title: Designing compassionate conversational AI: A preliminary Self Determination Theory framework for digital wellbeing

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Conversational Agents (CAs) is rapidly transforming higher education by providing personalised learning support, adaptive feedback, and interactive educational experiences. However, most research has focused on learning performance rather than students psychological wellbeing. This scoping review examines how Self-Determination Theory (SDT) has been applied in the design of conversational AI to promote digital wellbeing and compassionate educational technology. Guided by the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), a systematic search of four major databases identified 28 eligible studies published between 2018 and 2026. Thematic analysis revealed that conversational AI predominantly supports students competence through intelligent tutoring, adaptive scaffolding, and personalised feedback, while explicit support for autonomy and relatedness remains limited. Digital wellbeing is rarely considered an intended design outcome. Based on these findings, the review proposes a preliminary SDT informed conversational AI design framework comprising four interconnected principles which are supporting learner autonomy, strengthening competence, fostering relatedness through compassionate interactions, and promoting responsible AI use to enhance digital wellbeing. Integrating motivational psychology with human-centred AI design, this review provides practical guidance for developing AI systems that support learner agency, psychological wellbeing, and sustainable engagement, contributing to the design of compassionate educational technologies for the future of higher education.

items.abstract_text: This study examines how awareness of generative AI academic integrity policies shapes student anxiety, ethical reasoning, and writing practices in higher education. Drawing on a reflexive thematic analysis of student discourse from YouTube and Reddit, the study explores how detection-oriented governance frameworks are experienced and negotiated outside formal institutional contexts. Findings indicate that students do not primarily describe intentional rule-breaking; instead, they articulate experiences of surveillance, uncertainty, and adaptation within assessment systems perceived as inconsistent and adversarial. Three interrelated themes are identified: surveillance anxiety and defensive authorship; normative dissonance and moral negotiation of AI use; and cognitive offloading, systemic strain, and declining trust in assessment integrity. Across these themes, AI policy awareness is shown to shape not only behavioural responses but also students’ affective and epistemic relationships with writing, authorship, and institutional authority. The study argues that detection-first approaches risk intensifying anxiety and undermining trust without resolving underlying tensions in assessment design. It concludes that generative AI exposes structural fragilities in higher education, suggesting the need to reorient academic integrity governance toward design-led, transparent, and equity-sensitive approaches that prioritise learning, trust, and student experience.

items.abstract_text: Senior high school students increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), yet its link to higher-order thinking skills (HOTS) appears to depend on how the technology is used. This study examined the relationships between three GenAI use patterns (productive, metacognitive, and passive) and students' HOTS, as well as the mediating roles of digital creativity, learning agency, and academic engagement, controlling for AI literacy and ethical AI use. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed with 200 eleventh-grade students of SMA Negeri 1 Kutorejo, Mojokerto, selected through proportionate stratified random sampling from a population of 352, followed by semi-structured interviews with 25 purposively selected informants. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression with HC3 robust standard errors, and parallel mediation with 2,000 bootstrap resamples; qualitative data were analysed thematically. Metacognitive use showed the highest mean (M = 3.59), followed by productive (M = 3.45) and passive use (M = 2.66). The model explained 41.0% of the variance in HOTS (R² = .410). Metacognitive (B = 4.42) and productive use (B = 2.76) were positively associated with HOTS, whereas passive use was negatively associated (B = −2.45), all p ≤ .001. Digital creativity was the only significant mediator, for both productive (indirect effect = 0.47) and metacognitive use (0.28), unlike learning agency and academic engagement. Interview themes on verification strategies and dependency were consistent with these patterns. How students use GenAI, rather than whether they use it, matters for HOTS, and creative, verification-oriented use deserves pedagogical support.

items.abstract_text: Este estudio analiza el impacto de un asistente socrático de inteligencia artificial en el Modelo Heutagógico Unadista Solidario 5.0 de la UNAD. El objetivo principal fue evaluar la adopción tecnológica y el impacto pedagógico de esta herramienta en el aprendizaje del modelado de software (UML) mediante el caso de estudio Webmed. La investigación empleó un enfoque cuantitativo descriptivo basado en la Teoría Unificada de Aceptación y Uso de Tecnología, aplicado a una muestra de 18 estudiantes de ingeniería de sistemas. Los resultados indican una aceptación favorable con un promedio de 3.87/5.0, donde el 83% de los participantes reportó mejoras significativas en su rapidez operativa y comprensión de diagramas. No obstante, se identificaron riesgos críticos relacionados con la dependencia cognitiva y la falta de verificación de fuentes, ya que solo el 53% contrastó las respuestas con la bibliografía oficial del curso. Se concluye que el asistente funciona como un andamiaje efectivo que potencia la autodeterminación y el aprendizaje autodirigido, reduciendo barreras de abstracción técnica. Sin embargo, su efectividad integral depende de la implementación de estrategias de alfabetización algorítmica que mitiguen la pereza metacognitiva y aseguren una integración ética y crítica de la inteligencia artificial en los ecosistemas educativos híbridos de la UNAD 5.0.

items.title: Beyond the tool: a systematic realist synthesis of cognitive agency in human-GenAI interaction in higher education
items.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Cognitive agency concerns learners’ effortful, self-directed control over reasoning with generative AI (GenAI). Building on an existing implementation-level classification of generative AI use, this review examines how cognitive work is allocated between learners and AI tools. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Scopus and Web of Science (2021–2025) yielded 93 peer-reviewed studies, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A realist synthesis specified an a priori program theory crossing the type of work offloaded (extraneous versus germane; cognitive load theory) with processing of AI output (heuristic acceptance versus analytical scrutiny; dual-process theory), and audited the evidence on each axis under manifest coding (reported evidence only) and latent coding (adding design-based inference). Under manifest coding, 21 studies were located on both axes; all four configurations occurred, two in a single study each, and the nine Cognitive Extension studies reported peripheral uses with analytical scrutiny. Of the 93 studies, 49 reported no learner behavior toward AI output, 69 reported no learning measure independent of AI assistance, and four reported processing evidence together with such a measure. Group differences or part-sample outcomes were documented in 30 studies; one further study reported stage differences, but no learner-, task-, or assessment-level moderator showed an interpretable corpus-level association with substitution. This evidence profile identifies the process and AI-independent learning measures needed to distinguish cognitive extension from cognitive substitution. The review restates the Heterogeneous Pathways of Distributed Agency (HPDA) Model as seven testable propositions and specifies the process-tracing and AI-independent outcome designs needed to test them.

items.title: What is Hybrid Intelligence? Toward a Multi-Layered Model for Complex Problem-Solving
items.venue: International Journal of Technology in Teaching and Learning

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The dominant automation paradigm, which measures artificial intelligence by its capacity to act independently of humans, is increasingly inadequate for complex problem-solving. This article develops the concept of Hybrid Intelligence, defined as an adaptive, self-regulating system arising from the synergistic integration of human and artificial intelligence to enhance cognitive abilities. Revisiting the cognitive-tools tradition through an information-processing lens, it argues that generative AI dissolves the safeguard that once ensured tools amplified rather than supplanted human thinking. It then specifies a layered, multi-agentic architecture in which AI agents and agentic AI are embedded within contextual and collaborative human layers. It applies this architecture to the phases of complex problem-solving. The overriding argument is that sustainable Hybrid Intelligence requires enduring theoretical foundations that outlast individual model releases, ensuring that human–AI collaboration genuinely enhances, rather than inadvertently constrains, human cognitive agency.

items.title: When AI makes learning feel effortless: how processing fluency shapes students’ metacognitive judgments

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make learning feel easier, but whether this ease helps students accurately judge what they have learned remains unclear. Drawing on the cue-utilization framework, this research examines processing fluency as a metacognitive mechanism linking GenAI-assisted learning to judgments of learning (JOLs) and calibration. Across three experiments with university students, we tested how AI assistance, explanation fluency, and unaided retrieval shape subjective learning judgments relative to subsequent independent test performance. Study 1 ( N = 264) showed that GenAI-assisted learning increased processing fluency and JOLs, with a significant indirect association linking AI assistance to JOLs through processing fluency. Study 2 ( N = 360) manipulated fluency in scripted AI explanations delivered through a simulated GenAI interface and compared them with conventional-text learning. High-fluency explanations elicited higher JOLs and greater positive calibration bias than low-fluency explanations and conventional-text learning, although the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in objective test performance. Absolute calibration error did not differ significantly across conditions. Study 3 ( N = 386) showed that a brief no-AI retrieval attempt substantially weakened the relationship between processing fluency and JOL and reduced overall positive calibration bias. However, the retrieval-related reduction in calibration bias did not differ significantly between the high and low-fluency conditions. Together, the findings suggest that GenAI can shape metacognitive judgments by changing how fluent learning feels, while the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in immediate independent test performance. Providing learners with opportunities for unaided retrieval may help shift judgments from AI-generated processing ease toward more diagnostic evidence of what they can independently retrieve.

items.abstract_text: While AI is rapidly reshaping higher education by offering greater accessibility, personalized learning, and enhanced student engagement, its adoption often surpasses institutional capacity to adapt governance, pedagogy, and knowledge practices. This study, part of an ongoing collaboration between the University of North Carolina Wilmington (USA) and the University of Hertfordshire (UK), explores the practical integration of AI in higher education and proposes an Artificial Intelligence Readiness Framework to support curriculum design, assessment, governance, and knowledge management. The paper presents an exploratory case study of guided AI use in a large postgraduate taught module involving over 300+ international students at the University of Hertfordshire Business School. Drawing on module-level secondary data and instructor reflections, the study examines student engagement with AI, challenges encountered, and implications for teaching and assessment practice. Preliminary findings suggest that structured AI integration within active learning activities supported idea generation, writing development, and student engagement. However, instructor observations also indicated that some students relied on AI-generated content without sufficient critical evaluation, resulting in weaker alignment with assessment expectations. While students generally disclosed their use of AI, concerns remained regarding overreliance and the development of critical thinking skills. The study offers preliminary practitioner insights and introduces an AI Readiness Framework to support the responsible and pedagogically informed integration of AI into higher education curricula.

items.title: GenAI avatars to promote negotiation and AI skills among student presentations

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has radically disrupted higher education assessment paradigms (Chung, 2024). Institutional responses to maintaining assessment integrity have primarily focused on defensive mechanisms, such as mitigating risks surrounding written assessments, refining text-matching software, and enforcing restrictive academic integrity policies (Lodge, 2024). However, this reactive posture often overlooks the transformative potential of GenAI as a student’s and lecturer’s long-term coach in authentic assessment design (Atif, 2024). This research-in-progress pivots away from deficit-based AI detection, proposing instead the integration of VirtualSpeech GenAI avatars to converse with students during a recorded viva, generating verifiable, real-time student output. By replacing static written tasks with dynamic oral assessments, this relatively new form of creative expression maintains authentic student contributions to improve AI literacy, strengthen authorship verification, eliminate academic outsourcing, and simultaneously cultivate sophisticated negotiation skills (Perkins, 2026). This study represents an exemplary innovation of practice by reframing AI not as an academic threat, but as a dual-mode learning and assessment avatar. Rather than engaging with AI purely for text generation, students interact with GenAI avatars (such as VirtualSpeech) simulating realistic corporate stakeholders. This work is strongly anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which guides the deliberate alignment of GenAI technology, modern pedagogy, and discipline-specific knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). This framework assists educators in leveraging immersive technology to redefine pedagogical delivery, facilitating AI literacy and negotiation skills. This research addresses a critical gap in current Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) literature by investigating the following central question: How are students’ AI literacy and negotiation skills developed when conversing with GenAI avatars as part of a viva presentation? Adopting a design-based research methodology, this project emphasizes the iterative refinement of an educational intervention within an authentic setting (Hoadley & Campos, 2022; Scott et al., 2020). The study is currently in its first implementation cycle within a major tertiary institution, featuring a sample size of 150 second-year Project Management students. Participants are required to defend a project proposal during a live, assessable viva presentation conducted with a customized VirtualSpeech avatar trained to act as a client. This oral format diminishes the appeal of cognitive offloading because students must defend their reasoning under unseen, real-time questioning (Sotiriadou et al., 2020; Tan, 2026). Data collection relies on a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-intervention surveys alongside qualitative analysis of student reflections. Preliminary quantitative results indicate a statistically significant increase in both self-reported IT literacy, validating the avatar’s efficacy as a formative and summative tool. This research significantly advances TEL research and practice by providing a protocol for proactive AI integration. While piloted within a project management curriculum, broad applicability across tertiary contexts exists (Cela-Ranilla, 2025). Any discipline requiring high-stakes communication, critical thinking, and stakeholder management—such as business, law, or education—can adapt this viva model. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how universities can safeguard academic integrity not by restricting technology, but leveraging it to create robust, future-focused verbal assessments, requiring students to perform and defend understanding live.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based chatbots have the potential to serve as scaffolding in programming learning, but there are concerns that they may weaken students' independent thinking. This study examined the effectiveness of an AI chatbot within a Problem-Based Learning (PBL) model on the Moodle Learning Management System in improving the Computational Thinking (CT) of vocational high school students, by analyzing its effects according to prior ability and CT indicators. The study used a Research and Development approach based on the SLEEG framework and the ADDIE stages, with a one-group pretest–posttest design involving 39 tenth-grade students of the Software and Game Development program at SMK Negeri 11 Bandung. The media were rated highly feasible by the subject-matter expert (90.58%) and the media expert (90%). The mean score increased from 75.49 to 85.33, and the difference was significant (Wilcoxon test, Z = −3.615; p < 0.001) with an N-Gain of 0.40 (moderate). The largest improvement was found among students with low prior ability (N-Gain 0.56), whereas the high-ability group showed a decline in scores. Scores on Evaluation, Algorithmic Thinking, and Generalization increased, but Abstraction and Decomposition did not improve, which indicates cognitive offloading. Student responses were rated very good (89.31%). The AI chatbot appears effective as scaffolding at the problem-solving stage, so its use needs to be limited at the problem-identification stage.

items.title: From AI fatigue to compassionate practice: Building student AI literacy through continuous feedback and reflective practice

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) presents significant challenges in higher education, often leading to student dependency and educator “AI fatigue.” Despite policy calls for assessment reform, practical, evidence-based approaches to developing critical AI literacy remain limited. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a practice-based curriculum case study and reflective inquiry investigating the structural redesign of a multidisciplinary Information and Communications Technology (ICT) unit. Moving away from surveillance and AI detection, the curriculum was redesigned to decompose high-stakes assessments into a scaffolded, low-stakes formative feedback sequence. Employing a Reflective Teaching Practice (RTP) methodology grounded in Schön’s reflective practitioner framework, the inquiry evaluates this curriculum redesign through the educator’s professional reflective diary and theoretical student persona modelling. Theoretical learning archetypes were constructed to evaluate how the scaffolded structures support diverse student AI literacy profiles. Educator reflective logs highlighted strategies for managing AI dependency and inflated expectations around AI, suggesting that scaffolded AI literacy and personally relevant assessments helped mitigate cognitive offloading. Ultimately, this inquiry suggests that navigating the AI landscape requires a return to foundational, compassionate pedagogical principles, prioritising continuous feedback and structured self-reflection to support positioning AI as a meaningful learning opportunity rather than a disruptive academic burden.

items.title: Beyond Operational Fluency: A Three-Tier AI Literacy Architecture for Reskilling and Upskilling in Strategic Talent Development
items.venue: International Journal of AI in Pedagogy Innovation and Learning Futures

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.abstract_text: Higher education largely frames generative AI (GAI) as a productivity tool, overlooking a relational problem: how globally distributed student teams build shared understanding and trust. This paper reports on two conversational AI bots built on BoodleBox and designed as “teammates” rather than assistants: AINO, used in an in-person Erasmus+ Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) in Finland, and Collaboration Cosmo, used in the eight-week, fully virtual Cosmogogy Collaborative (CosCollab). Drawing on Cosmogogy’s Human-AI-World ecosystem, we argue that an AI teammate’s value lies as much in the relational infrastructure it holds (memory, mediation, inclusion) as in its outputs. Analysis of CosCollab chat logs identified the roles Cosmo assumed, while reflexive thematic analysis of BIP focus group and reflection data revealed four themes: expectation setting, bot dominance and the anthropomorphisation paradox, language equity, and AI as instrumental partner versus formative presence. We propose design refinements for AI-embedded global collaboration.

items.title: Longitudinal association between AI dependence and pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition: the role of AI self-efficacy and perceived stress

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into teacher education has brought both opportunities and challenges. While AI tools are increasingly accessible to pre-service teachers, excessive dependence on AI may inadvertently undermine their critical thinking disposition—a key competency in professional development. Based on social cognitive theory, this study investigates the influence of AI dependence on pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition, with a particular focus on the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and the moderating role of perceived stress. A three-phase longitudinal design was employed. The study tracked 461 pre-service teachers from Jiangxi Province, China. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the hypothesized relationships, including the mediation effect of AI self-efficacy and the first-stage moderating effect of perceived stress. Results showed that AI dependence significantly and negatively predicted pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition. AI self-efficacy partially mediated this negative association. Furthermore, perceived stress significantly moderated the first stage of the mediation process, such that the negative association between AI dependence and AI self-efficacy was stronger among pre-service teachers with higher levels of perceived stress. The conditional indirect effect was stronger at higher levels of perceived stress, and the index of moderated mediation was significant. The second-stage moderation was not significant. These findings highlight the potential risks associated with excessive AI dependence in teacher education: over-reliance on AI may undermine pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition partly through reduced AI self-efficacy. Moreover, perceived stress amplifies the negative indirect effect by moderating the first stage of the mediation process. This study extends social cognitive theory to the context of AI use and provides practical implications for promoting balanced AI engagement and critical thinking development in teacher training programs.

items.title: Metacognitive Management of Human–AI Interaction: A Framework for Cognitive Delegation, Monitoring, and Independent Verification
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into intellectual activities is transforming how individuals acquire information, solve problems, generate ideas, and make decisions. Although these systems can substantially expand access to cognitive resources, their effectiveness depends not only on technological capabilities but also on users’ ability to regulate their own thinking during human–AI interaction. A central challenge is determining which cognitive activities should be performed independently, which can be delegated to artificial intelligence, and under what conditions AI-generated outputs require independent verification. This conceptual paper examines metacognitive management of human–AI interaction as a dynamic process involving cognitive self-awareness, strategic delegation, ongoing monitoring, critical evaluation, and reflective adjustment. Drawing on classical theories of metacognition, cognitive offloading, trust calibration, and contemporary research on human–AI collaboration, the paper proposes the Metacognitive Delegation and Verification Cycle (MDVC), a six-stage framework for regulating AI involvement in cognitive activities. The framework distinguishes between task execution and cognitive responsibility, arguing that effective delegation does not necessarily entail the abandonment of independent reasoning. Instead, appropriately regulated interaction allows individuals to distribute cognitive effort while preserving their capacity to evaluate evidence, recognize uncertainty, revise decisions, and maintain intellectual autonomy. The paper further introduces a task-sensitive delegation typology, a risk-adjusted verification strategy, and practical metacognitive questions designed to support users before, during, and after AI-assisted activities. Potential applications are examined in education, scientific research, professional reasoning, and everyday decision-making. Finally, testable propositions and methodological directions are presented for future empirical investigation. The central argument is that the development of human–AI collaboration should be evaluated not only through improvements in immediate task performance but also through the quality of cognitive regulation, independent understanding, and the preservation of human judgment

items.title: AI usage, large language model dependence, and critical thinking among university students: the mediating roles of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into higher education has intensified debate over how AI-assisted learning may be associated with students’ cognitive development. Although prior studies have examined the benefits and risks of AI use, less attention has been paid to the distinction between frequent AI usage as a learning behavior and large language model dependence (LLMD) as a habitual reliance on LLMs for cognitive and academic tasks. This study therefore distinguishes frequent AI usage as a learning behavior from LLMD as a habitual reliance on LLMs when completing cognitive and academic tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined how AI usage is associated with university students’ critical thinking through LLMD, metacognitive awareness, and AI literacy. Survey data were collected from 878 Chinese university students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with LLMD, which represented the strongest direct association in the model, while LLMD was negatively associated with metacognitive awareness, AI literacy, and critical thinking. The mediation analysis further indicated a significant negative total indirect association between AI usage and critical thinking through LLMD and lower levels of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy. These findings contribute to the literature by clarifying the distinction between AI usage and LLMD and by identifying metacognitive awareness and AI literacy as cognitive resources associated with critical thinking in AI-assisted learning contexts. Practically, the study suggests that universities should move beyond simple restriction-oriented responses and pay greater attention to the quality of students’ AI engagement, including metacognitive monitoring, AI literacy, and awareness of dependence-related patterns.

items.abstract_text: The rapid emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive supply chain orchestration, and real-time cross-border regulatory analytics is fundamentally transforming how multinational enterprises (MNEs) govern global value chains (GVCs) and enter foreign markets. Yet International Business (IB) higher education remains largely tethered to twentieth-century pedagogical paradigms—relying on static international trade models, retrospective written case studies, and essentialist cultural heuristics that fail to prepare graduates for algorithmically mediated global commerce. Moving beyond surface-level classroom adoption of generative chatbots, this study develops a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for re-engineering International Business education through the lenses of Global Value Chain Governance Theory, Activity Theory, and Metacognitive Scaffolding. We argue that the defining competency for next-generation IB professionals is Algorithmic Value-Chain Orchestration—the ability to align predictive and generative AI systems with cross-jurisdictional institutional realities, geopolitical risks, and culturally grounded human judgment. To operationalize this capability, the paper introduces a Three-Horizon Curricular Transformation Architecture alongside a Synthetic Global Commerce Laboratory that immerses students in dynamic multi-tier supply chain disruptions, automated customs and rules-of-origin auditing, and cross-cultural digital platform governance. Drawing upon longitudinal pedagogical implementations across undergraduate and postgraduate IB cohorts, we demonstrate significant gains in students' systemic risk reasoning, critical verification of algorithmic outputs, and cross-border strategic adaptability. Finally, the study examines structural challenges—including cognitive atrophy, Western-centric training data biases, and cross-border data compliance—and establishes an institutional governance charter for sustainable business school transformation.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative and agentic systems, is rapidly reshaping higher education. This article examines the main changes AI is introducing in teaching, learning, assessment, research, and institutional operations. Drawing on recent empirical studies and reviews up to 2026, it shows that AI enables personalised learning, faster feedback, and greater accessibility, while also creating serious risks of cognitive offloading, weakened critical thinking, academic integrity problems, and equity gaps. The central argument is that the value of AI depends less on the technology itself than on deliberate pedagogical design, AI literacy, and institutional policies that keep human judgement and independent thinking at the centre. The goal is to help universities and students use AI as a powerful support tool rather than as a substitute for learning.

items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Reliance on AI-supported health recommendations is consequential, but a single behavioral source-selection decision is not equivalent to multidimensional psychological trust. Biosignals may contain predictive information before a choice, although small-sample multimodal models require leakage-free evaluation and cautious interpretation. PURPOSE: This study evaluated whether facial-expression probabilities and galvanic skin response (GSR) features predict a task-specific binary choice of an AI-labeled rather than doctor-labeled recommendation in a simulated ADHD assessment. The outcome is treated as a behavioral indicator of reliance rather than a direct measure of psychological trust. Method: This cross-sectional laboratory analysis included a cohort of 60 participants (40 AI-labeled and 20 doctor-labeled choices). Eight facial-expression probabilities and two GSR phasic features were evaluated in prespecified Early (6-3 s) and Proximal (3-0 s) windows. Ten repeats of participant-level stratified five-fold cross-validation were used. Scaling and SMOTETomek resampling occurred only within training folds, and the logistic stacking meta-learner was trained on strictly cross-fitted base-model probabilities. Model-specific 95% confidence intervals and paired AUC differences were estimated with 10,000 stratified participant bootstrap samples; five paired tests were Holm-adjusted. RESULTS: Early-window ROC-AUCs were 0.643 (95% CI 0.490-0.786) for Face, 0.430 (0.287-0.578) for GSR, and 0.526 (0.375-0.679) for stacking. Proximal-window ROC-AUCs were 0.550 (0.399-0.699), 0.381 (0.240-0.530), and 0.376 (0.229-0.529), respectively. Stacking did not outperform either modality. Early stacking was worse than Early Face (ΔAUC = -0.116, 95% CI -0.183 to -0.056; Holm-adjusted p = 0.002); the other adjusted paired comparisons were not significant. CONCLUSION: Multimodal stacking did not improve prediction in this small exploratory sample. These results do not establish either a general advantage or a lack of value of multimodal fusion. They do not support deployment or direct trust detection. Larger studies with verified synchronization, repeated decisions, independent trust measures, and external validation are required.

Using a design-based research (DBR) approach, this paper reports on the first iteration of three agents intended to support key challenges facing nursing education. publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

items.abstract_text: Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming ubiquitous in consumers' lives and search activities. AI applications that can create content, have conversations, respond to emotions, recognize images and objects, and construct real‐world experiences (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Google Lens, Apple Vision Pro) are transforming consumer search by functioning as psychological surrogates that assume key cognitive, evaluative, perceptual, and relational processes on consumers' behalf. Yet limited research has examined how these technologies transform the psychological mechanisms underlying consumer search. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic narrative review of 75 articles on the psychological foundations of consumer search and introduces the concept of AI psychological surrogacy, which happens when advanced‐AI technologies assume key psychological processes traditionally performed by humans. We develop a conceptual framework that theorizes AI psychological surrogacy across three higher‐order systems (affective‐relational delegation, cognitive‐evaluative substitution, and sensory‐perceptual construction) and six mechanisms: affective transference, relational surrogacy, cognitive delegation, evaluative surrogacy, perceptual offloading, and sensory augmentation. We advance six research propositions and a research agenda for investigating how reliance on AI as a psychological surrogate may alter consumer cognition, evaluation, perception, and relational dynamics.

items.abstract_text: Introduction: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can minimise large language model hallucinations while supporting self-regulated learning. We evaluated the impact of student engagement with a grounded RAG-AI tool (Google NotebookLM) on formative and internal assessment scores in undergraduate pathology, validated a 3-item AI Disclosure Form, and explored cognitive adoption barriers. Methods In a 12-week longitudinal study using an interrupted time series design, Phase II medical students (N = 211) received curated NotebookLM modules alongside core lectures. Students completed weekly quizzes, a 3-item disclosure form assessing the frequency, application mode, and trust in the AI resources, and end-of-study mixed-method questionnaires. Longitudinal cohorts were classified into High, Low, Inconsistent, and non-usage groups, with differences evaluated via ANOVA. Results The 3-item disclosure form demonstrated high reliability. The average scores of formative quizzes (p = 0.656) and summative internal exams (p = 0.961) did not differ significantly between the engagement groups. However, there were notable differences in performance during some of the dense, complex sections (Lung, p < 0.001; Renal, p < 0.001). Frequent users used active Socratic chat and self-quizzing to handle high cognitive demands. In contrast, inconsistent users showed "cognitive flight" under stress, and non-respondents scored significantly lower (24.83 ± 13.76). Conclusion A standalone RAG-AI tool does not automatically improve the overall performance of a group. Instead, it helps manage cognitive load during demanding modules for learners who are good at self-regulated learning. Future use needs structured workflows within a Learning Management System and training for prompt verification.

items.abstract_text: This study examined the effects of Generative AI (GenAI)-assisted learning on the critical thinking skills of higher secondary school students. A quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test design with a non-equivalent control group was used. The sample consisted of 59 Grade XII students of Garrison Academy Kharian Cantt (Army Public School and College), Punjab, Pakistan: 28 girls in the experimental group and 31 boys in the control group. For one month, the experimental group was taught with GenAI tools (Claude and DeepSeek) and the control group was taught with traditional methods. Critical thinking was measured before and after the teaching period with a 30-item Critical Thinking Questionnaire based on Facione's (1990) six skills: interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, and self-regulation. The data were analysed with paired-samples t-tests, independent-samples t-tests on gain scores, and analysis of covariance. The total critical thinking score of the experimental group rose from M = 72.71 (SD = 5.11) to M = 121.25 (SD = 7.79), t(27) = 29.02, p < .001, d = 7.37, and that of the control group rose from M = 68.68 (SD = 7.75) to M = 77.58 (SD = 8.03), t(30) = 8.15, p < .001, d = 1.13. The mean gain of the experimental group (48.54 points) was significantly larger than that of the control group (8.90 points), t(57) = 20.21, p < .001, d = 5.27, and the analysis of covariance, which adjusted for the pre-test score, gave the same result, F(1, 56) = 466.24, p < .001, partial η² = .893. All six skills improved more in the experimental group. For classroom practice, the result suggests that guided GenAI activities, in which students compare AI answers, check them against the textbook, and give their own reasons, are worth adding to regular teaching under the teacher's supervision. The effect sizes were unusually large, the experimental group also started higher than the control group (p = .023), and the pre-test reliability of the questionnaire was low (α = .29). The findings should be read with care because the groups were intact classes that also differed in gender. Keywords: Generative AI, Critical Thinking Skills, Higher Secondary Students, Quasi-Experimental Study

items.venue: International Journal of Latest Technology in Engineering Management & Applied Science

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering adult and continuing education, where it can explain, summarise, draft and evaluate on the learner's behalf. The quality of work produced with AI assistance may therefore rise while the learner's own understanding, judgement and critical thinking remain unchanged or decline. This conceptual article examines how AI-assisted adult learning can preserve learner autonomy, independent judgement and critical thinking while still benefiting from generative tools. It builds on Natseva's distinction between functional cognitive offloading and higher-order cognitive outsourcing and integrates it with research on learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, metacognition, automation bias, critical-thinking instruction and the learning–performance distinction, drawing on a purposive, non-systematic literature selection that is reported transparently. Because most empirical studies of generative AI in education involve school or university students, the article distinguishes evidence by learner population and discusses its transferability to adult education. The original contribution is the AI-Assisted Autonomy and Critical Thinking Assessment (AACTA) framework, which specifies six assessable dimensions: prior independent reasoning, purposeful AI engagement, appraisal of AI output, cross-source contrast, decision ownership, and unaided demonstration and transfer. Each dimension is operationalised as a scoring rubric with observable indicators at three levels, from displaced to autonomous, together with a procedure for training two assessors and checking their agreement. AACTA is compared with existing measures of learner autonomy, self-regulated learning and critical thinking. The framework is accompanied by a dual-outcome principle, which requires AI-assisted performance and unaided learning to be measured separately, and by a provisional assistance-gap index. Five testable hypotheses are formulated, and a three-arm randomised study with a preceding pilot and multi-context replication is proposed as future work. The framework has not been empirically validated, and no data were collected for this article.

items.abstract_text: This scoping review examines how AI literacy is connected to AI-supported problem solving in education. Drawing on 33 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025, the review maps study characteristics, AI literacy dimensions, problem-solving types, and reported information behaviors. Findings show that AI-supported problem solving is a rapidly expanding interdisciplinary area, with the largest concentrations in STEM, computer science, and teacher education. AI tools most often supported design, decision-making, and diagnosis-solution problems. However, AI literacy was commonly represented through knowing and using AI, while the combined Evaluate and Create AI dimension and AI Ethics were less consistently represented, and verification and trust calibration were seldom explicitly analyzed. The review reframes AI literacy as question-centered information behavior (IB), emphasizing how learners identify information needs, formulate questions, check AI outputs, verify accuracy, and use information ethically. This perspective highlights good questioning as central to responsible AI-supported learning and problem solving.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Critical thinking has been a cornerstone of education. Some wonder what these technological advancements will do to people’s thinking and, more specifically, to critical thinking. In this chapter, we look at some of the potential affordances and limitations to critical thinking regarding artificial intelligence (AI) and how educators might respond. We address three aspects of critical thinking as outlined by research. First, critical thinking is the capacity to problem-solve. AI has the potential to help solve problems, although it might also erode one’s abilities, what some researchers call “cognitive offloading.” Second, critical thinking is a social process where people come together to think and challenge ideas. AI and newer technologies in general might bring people together; however, they might lead to what we are calling social offloading. Third, critical thinking is dependent on a diversity of ideas. Generative AI has the potential to synthesize a diversity of information and provide greater access; however, its models and algorithms may slowly limit this diversity. We situate these conceptions of critical thinking in concert with AI and provide pedagogical considerations for music educators to move toward a more process-based approach to critical thinking. This includes creating purposeful moments for students to work collaboratively—or to gather—and think critically, while also using AI tools.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI could improve physicians' clinical performance, yet its use in medical training raises questions about whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use AI effectively and independently. We conducted a longitudinal randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students (389 analysed). Students completed clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were randomised to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the AI assistant, the AI assistant followed by scaffolding, or both simultaneously. AI scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their reasoning without providing direct answers; the assistant provided requested information and answers. The study comprised an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn. Frontier large language models (LLMs) completed the same tasks as an additional benchmark. Students initially performed below LLMs but later exceeded them following the interventions. Students who began with AI scaffolding achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than those given access to the AI assistant from the outset both during the subsequent intervention phase (75.2% vs 66.0%; OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12–2.68]) and after withdrawal (24.6% vs 14.4%; OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15–4.14]). After withdrawal, scaffold-first groups were the only groups to outperform both unsupported students (24.5–24.7% vs 9.0%; ORs 3.77–3.87, 95% CIs [1.25–12.00]) and LLMs (24.5–24.7% vs 8.6%; ORs 3.48–3.50, 95% CIs [1.22–9.89]). Introducing the AI assistant after scaffolding decreased intrinsic cognitive load ( t (50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and increased metacognitive evaluation ( t (50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). These findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding precedes answer-providing assistance to strengthen diagnostic performance both during AI-supported learning and after AI support is withdrawn.

items.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly entering translator education, yet it remains unclear whether they build students' own translation competence or merely improve the products students submit. We combined a validation study on public benchmark data with a 16-week quasi-experiment to test a scaffolded human--LLM pedagogy, the Draft--Diagnose--Revise--Reflect (D2R) cycle, for English--Chinese translation. In Study 1, a rubric-guided error-annotation prompt increased the agreement between LLM feedback and expert Multidimensional Quality Metrics judgements on 2,500 WMT segments for all four models tested; with this prompt GPT-4o reached a segment-level Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.30, on a par with the strongest neural metric, and the highest error-detection accuracy. In Study 2, 179 English majors received conventional instruction, unrestricted LLM access or the guardrailed D2R cycle. Unrestricted access maximised LLM-assisted performance but yielded no advantage in unassisted translation over conventional instruction at a delayed test 12 weeks after the course (Hedges' $g$ = $-$0.08) and produced the largest AI-dependency gap. Scaffolded use produced durable gains in unassisted translation ($g$ = 0.70), a 13\% reduction in error rate and higher metacognitive regulation. Process logs indicated that the benefit was transmitted mainly through lower verbatim adoption of LLM output. Pedagogical design, not LLM access per se, determines whether LLMs support or supplant translation learning.

items.abstract_text: This paper reports preliminary findings from a redesigned capstone assessment in a first-year Management unit at an Australian university involving over 300 students. Rather than treating generative AI as a content-generation tool, the assessment positions it as a simulated interview partner within a three-phase architecture: a pre-interview strategy memo, an AI-conducted adaptive interview, and a post-interview reflective analysis. Grounded in Schön’s reflective practice framework and Biggs and Tang’s constructive alignment, the design surfaces the gap between how students plan to communicate and how they do. Preliminary thematic analysis of 21 student reflective submissions reveals four patterns: (a) the strategy memo functions as a metacognitive anchor, making the gap between intention and execution visible and diagnosable; (b) students consistently demonstrate framework knowledge but revert to habitual communication patterns under adaptive pressure; (c) the structured reflection phase produces sophisticated self-diagnostic reasoning that connects transcript evidence to communication theory; and (d) students who completed multiple simulation attempts used iterative practice as a developmental mechanism rather than a remedial exercise. These findings suggest that AI-simulated interviews, when embedded within a reflective assessment architecture, generate qualitatively richer professional learning than traditional scripted interview preparation.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning practices, yet its implications for student well-being remain insufficiently explored. This literature review synthesizes existing evidence on the potential benefits and risks of generative AI use for university student well-being and examines the psychological mechanisms that may explain these relationships. The reviewed literature suggests that when generative AI is used as a learning-support tool, it may contribute to reduced academic stress, stronger learning confidence, greater learning efficiency, emotional support, and greater satisfaction with task completion. In contrast, when AI substitutes for rather than supports core cognitive processes, its use may be associated with over-reliance, diminished autonomous learning, academic-integrity concerns, AI-related employment anxiety, and technostress. Self-efficacy, cognitive offloading, academic stress, and autonomy emerge as important psychological mechanisms through which generative AI use may relate to student well-being. Overall, the relationship between generative AI use and student well-being does not appear to be uniformly beneficial or harmful but varies according to how, why, and to what extent students use AI. Future research should therefore move beyond whether students use generative AI and examine more precisely the patterns and conditions of use that support or undermine student well-being.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative AI poses a risk to students’ creative thinking when it is adopted without critical reflection (Elgammal, 2026). These tools are marketed as collaborators and tutors, offering constant and largely uncritical encouragement (Chow & Celis Bueno, 2025; Walsh 2025). This presentation holds the promise of AI partnership alongside evidence that these tools displace cognitive and creative effort (Gerlich, 2025; Temler 2026). This problem is widely recognised, but proposed responses remain inconsistent, vague or untested. Many calls to address the use of generative AI correctly identify the problem or alternatively show singular approaches and case studies. What is needed is a discipline-agnostic framework on building students’ awareness of their own creative processes in the context of these tools. The approach offered here to develop creativity with AI has two theoretical foundations: Margaret Boden’s theory of creativity and art, and the Kolb Experiential Learning Cycle (2011) as a pedagogical approach. Boden (2004 distinguishes combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity: the recombination of existing ideas, movement within a conceptual space, and alteration of that space’s defining dimensions. Novelty can be either new to the individual or new more generally under this view. Boden argues that novelty may come about in several ways, including combining existing ideas in new ways, exploring or changing existing ideas, or transforming dimensions of those ideas. The two frameworks do different work. Boden supplies the criteria students apply when judging whether their output is genuinely novel, surprising and valuable; Kolb supplies the cycle through which that judgement is made repeatedly and acted upon. Without Boden, reflection has no object; without Kolb, the criteria are applied once and forgotten. Students work through Kolb’s (2011) four stages in their learning: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation. These each serve a cumulative purpose in developing the students’ collaborative process with generative AI. In the first phase, the student does their first draft of a creative process, using AI in any way they want to experiment with. Afterward, they reflect on that experience, considering questions about what skills they developed (or did not), whether the draft did what they wanted it to do, and how they felt about the AI tool use. Based on this reflection, they can then develop and express a personal set of beliefs on practical use of generative AI. Finally, they can try out a new approach based on these conclusions – which then become the next concrete experience. It is an ongoing and cyclical process of practical experimentation and personal reflection. The framework is adapted from the “Creativity and AI” module of Sage’s Digital Literacy course (Zaphir & Henrickson, in press). Its purpose is to be discipline agnostic; a framework which can be broadly applicable across cohorts and disciplines. Critical AI literacies require the development of students’ own ethical ideas and practical skills in using the tools; this process is designed to be adaptable in any context. Creativity has different implications and different applications in each discipline. AI can act as a useful collaborator if the user can state what and why they want to do it. Students will all benefit in the exercise of deliberately choosing which skills to offload and which to augment, and then reflecting on their choices with each use. The presentation works through one complete turn of the cycle using a worked example: the initial AI-assisted draft, the reflective prompts applied to it, the position statement the student produced, and the changed approach taken on the next attempt. Slides alternate between student artefacts and the framework stage they illustrate. Attendees will leave with the reflection prompts used at each stage and a one-page cycle template they can adapt to their own discipline and cohort.

items.title: Friction by design – desirable difficulty in AI co-learning

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: AI is only the latest in a succession of educational technologies that have made learning easier and more frictionless, which, counterintuitively, has coincided with a population-level decline in cognitive ability and poor learning outcomes. Studies in cognitive offloading and productive struggle suggest it may be affordances of information technology exacerbated by AI that contribute to these poor outcomes. Describing the relevance of cognitive offloading, cognitive load theory and the expertise reversal effect, this paper explores the cognitive mechanisms associated with technological assistance that have been shown to affect learning, and considers pathways to redesign learning in a way that focuses on useful forms of learning friction, understood as the effortful work that consolidates learning. The paper locates these cognitive mechanisms near the learner experience where self-regulation holds the most potential to effect change when combined with educator support. The question for educators, designers and students will continue to evolve: does experiencing friction enhance learning? A heuristic is offered as a conceptual model of a process for teachers and designers to support learners at the point where cognitive offloading occurs.

items.title: HUMAN-AI SYMBIOSIS IN GLOBAL COMMERCE EDUCATION: INSTITUTIONAL ADAPTATION, CURRICULUM CO-EVOLUTION, AND EXPERIENTIAL PEDAGOGY IN INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive trade analytics, and multimodal generative models into multinational enterprise (MNE) operations has fundamentally disrupted the foundational assumptions of International Business (IB) higher education. Traditional IB pedagogy—anchored in static comparative advantage models, retrospective case analyses, and isolated cross-cultural taxonomies—increasingly fails to prepare graduates for an era defined by algorithmic global value chains and geopolitical fragmentation. Moving beyond superficial classroom tool adoption, this study investigates how Artificial Intelligence can systematically restructure International Business education through the theoretical lenses of Institutional Entrepreneurship, Distributed Cognition, and Experiential Learning Theory. We argue that modern global business education must cultivate Symbiotic Cross-Border Intelligence—the integrated capacity to deploy, audit, and ethically govern intelligent systems across divergent sovereign, cultural, and regulatory jurisdictions. To operationalize this paradigm, the paper constructs an Adaptive Curriculum Co-Evolution Model paired with a Four-Tiered Experiential Learning Ecosystem that replaces passive lecturing with live cross-border algorithmic sandboxes, regulatory friction wargames, and multilingual stakeholder simulations. Drawing upon multi-semester pedagogical implementations across international finance, global supply chain resilience, and emerging-market entry courses, we demonstrate substantial improvements in students’ causal systems reasoning, hallucination forensics, and cross-cultural communicative agility. Finally, the paper addresses structural risks—including algorithmic monoculture, epistemic dependency, and extraterritorial data governance violations—and formulates an institutional compliance charter for business schools navigating the intelligent transformation of global commerce.

items.title: Capability atrophy: When AI automation erodes the dynamic capabilities it was meant to build

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Firms adopt artificial intelligence (AI) automation to strengthen their dynamic capabilities, yet automation can also remove managers from the routines through which those capabilities are renewed. Drawing on the microfoundations of dynamic capabilities, organizational learning theory, and the automation–augmentation paradox, this conceptual paper develops the concept of capability atrophy and specifies when AI automation weakens, rather than builds, firm-level dynamic capabilities. Theory synthesis across research on skill erosion, organizational learning, and human–AI collaboration yields nine propositions, together with a multilevel, multi-wave mixed-methods design that uses behavioral and system-discontinuance measures to test them. The propositions hold that automation intensity relates to dynamic capability change in an inverted-U pattern, turning negative beyond a substitution threshold. Erosion travels through reduced experiential engagement, weaker skill retention, and poorer reliance calibration, and it becomes organizational when tacit knowledge is concentrated and apprenticeship paths close. Retained decision roles, frequent exceptions, and task variety are proposed to raise the threshold, whereas analytics capability alone is not. The paper places capability atrophy within existing skill-erosion research and adds a firm-level, conditional account with explicit falsification criteria. For practice, it implies that managers should track override rates, unaided diagnosis time, and other observable indicators of capability retention alongside the returns on AI investment.

items.title: Mitochondrial capacity limits neuronal energetic feasibility under chronic behavioural stress associated with AI-intensive environments: a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Abstract Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.
