items.title: Beyond Operational Fluency: A Three-Tier AI Literacy Architecture for Reskilling and Upskilling in Strategic Talent Development
items.venue: International Journal of AI in Pedagogy Innovation and Learning Futures

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This review synthesizes evidence from recent studies of human–AI collaboration in service and digital ecosystems to build and test a multi-level conceptual framework. Design/methodology/approach: Thirteen studies (Tier A) from 2024 to 2026 were analyzed in full text and compared with 25 qualitative and mixed-methods studies (Tier B). In total, 38 service and digital ecosystem studies were analyzed within this review. Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and the Affect–Behavior–Cognition (ABC) model was used as the underlying theoretical framework. Narrative and thematic analysis were employed to synthesize the results from the included studies. Findings: Transparency, process control and outcome control have significant effects on employees in terms of cognitive and behavioral effects, while system-initiated engagement has little effect. Human–AI interaction does not, on average, perform better than the best human in each task (g = ?0.23, p < .001), but does perform better than a single human in a variety of tasks (g = 0.64). Value is created through the integration of systems and not through technology itself. User experience, digital maturity, interoperable IT, and AI-induced technostress condition value realization. Originality/value: The study provides a three-stage framework, seven testable hypotheses, seven gaps in current research and an operational measurement for value creation at the employee level and for firm- and network-level value co-creation.

items.title: Sparse Attention for Visual Generation: Toward Algorithm-System Co-Design

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.

items.title: Synergising Lean construction and artificial intelligence: a conceptual framework

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Purpose The integration of artificial intelligence with Lean construction has been shown to promote added value and drive growth in the built environment. However, understanding of their interaction across multiple levels of abstraction remains limited, especially beyond technical optimisation. This article systematically reviews the interaction between AI and Lean construction to identify current interactions, major applications and research gaps. Design/methodology/approach Following the PRISMA protocol, 63 peer-reviewed studies were identified and analysed qualitatively. AI techniques were mapped against Lean construction principles, waste categories and Lean methods to enable a multi-level comparative synthesis. Findings The results show a growing interest over the past four years, with a focus on AI techniques such as machine learning, optimisation and computer vision used to enhance workflow and to reduce cycle times, particularly within the Last Planner System. Nonetheless, principles centred on value creation, collaboration and partner development remain largely underexplored. Similarly, a co-adaptive relationship was observed to be emerging, in which AI improves Lean's technical efficiency while Lean principles guide AI's development towards ethical and value-driven outcomes. Research limitations/implications The findings offer a foundation for advancing Lean Construction 4.0 through socio-technical integration and human-centred innovation. Practitioners can start by applying mature AI techniques to improve measurable Lean outcomes such as workflow reliability, constraint prediction, visual management and waste reduction, then extend GenAI and NLP tools to collaboration, requirement capture, knowledge reuse and cross-project learning. Originality/value The study proposes a dual-focus model that separates AI's current role as a technical enabler from its future potential as a holistic partner.

items.title: Who Controls the Revision When GenAI Gives Feedback? Evidence from Indonesian EFL Writers
items.venue: Indonesian Language Education and Applied Linguistics Reviews

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: This convergent mixed-methods multiple-case study examined how 16 Indonesian EFL undergraduates exercised revision agency while using generative-AI feedback across four connected writing tasks. The corpus comprised 64 final texts, 48.5 hours of screen recording, 342 prompt-response decision episodes, 16 interviews, stimulated recall, four focus-group reflections, and a 96-page analytic memo trail. Descriptive episode coding identified four patterns: selective scaffolding (38.6%), iterative co-composition (29.2%), surface repair (21.3%), and delegated composition (10.8%). Integrated qualitative analysis showed that high-agency use was marked by a bounded purpose, comparison of alternatives, transformation or rejection of output, verification, and the ability to defend the final text. High-proficiency students most often used selective scaffolding and rejected about 65% of outputs; intermediate students more often negotiated through iterative co-composition and rejected about 35%; low-intermediate students more often relied on surface repair or delegation and rejected about 10%. Frequency of AI use was therefore a weak indicator of learning or responsibility. Revision agency depended on what students did between receiving feedback and submitting text. The study contributes a process-based taxonomy and an evidence model for distinguishing assistance from substitution. It recommends bounded prompting, accept-modify-reject rationales, verification routines, teacher moderation, revision memos, and independent performance evidence.

items.abstract_text: This study investigates whether LLM-based Conversational Agents (LLMCAs) could be employed as assistive technologies, helping anyone navigate a website by explaining its content and interactive features, and suggesting actions to accomplish specific goals. This would make the web more accessible especially to seniors, blind users and people with mild cognitive impairment. Specifically, the study examines whether such tools can analyze the source code of a webpage to identify its structure and interactive elements, understand which interactive components are required to support users in achieving their goals, and act effectively as assistive technologies. In addition, the work compares leading tools to assess differences in their effectiveness and behavior in supporting accessible web interaction. The work presents two empirical studies in which four popular LLMCA tools are evaluated on a set of public websites, in order to assess their ability to understand web page structures and interactive components and assist users in their tasks. The evaluation combines qualitative and quantitative measures, focusing on accuracy, completeness, and practical usefulness of the responses.Results show a good degree of pertinent and good-quality answers, even on websites with a poorly accessible structure. The user-friendly way to interact with a LLMCA makes it much comfortable to use for the average user. However, the study also highlights that some LLMCAs appear more 'skilled' in accessibility tasks than others. LLMCAs show promising potential not only to complement existing assistive technologies but also to support or replace the human assistance that is often required for many users to effectively access the web.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: This study examines prompt literacy among future computer science teachers in the context of solving and debugging programming tasks with ChatGPT. It focuses on students' perceptions of prompt literacy, their understanding of responsible AI use, documented practices of verifying and modifying AI-assisted solutions, and patterns of academic performance. A descriptive multi-method study was conducted during a 16-week programming course involving 113 future computer science teachers at Kh. Dosmukhamedov Atyrau University, Kazakhstan. Data were collected through questionnaires, student programming submissions, ChatGPT-use disclosure notes, reflective comments, code-similarity screening, and course-grade records. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative content analysis was used to identify recurring patterns in students' reported use, verification, and revision of AI-generated solutions. The findings were compared across data sources to address the research questions without testing causal effects or participant-level associations. The 20-item Prompt-Literacy Perceptions Questionnaire demonstrated high overall internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.94). Students generally reported positive perceptions of ChatGPT for code generation, debugging, and explaining programming logic. They also recognized the importance of verifying AI-generated outputs and disclosing substantial AI assistance. However, students' documentation of verification and modification practices was frequently general rather than detailed. Pairwise code-similarity screening identified relatively few submission pairs exceeding the predefined 50% similarity threshold. Mean academic scores were numerically close across practical assignments and independent control tasks, although differences in assessment conditions and grading criteria limited direct comparisons. The findings highlight the importance of integrating prompt literacy, critical verification, and transparent documentation of AI use into computer science teacher education. Positive perceptions of responsible ChatGPT use did not necessarily correspond to detailed documentation of verification and revision practices. Code-similarity results cannot independently establish whether students modified AI-generated solutions. Furthermore, the descriptive single-cohort design does not support conclusions about causal effects or improvements in prompt-literacy competence. The study emphasizes the pedagogical value of making students' reasoning, verification, and responsible AI-use practices explicit during programming instruction.

items.abstract_text: Drawing on dynamic usage‐based and interactionist SLA perspectives, this study investigated developmental patterns of linguistic complexity and language‐related episodes (LREs) during L2 learners' written interactions with ChatGPT. Ten Korean EFL learners completed seven sessions of opinion‐gap and debate tasks over 5 weeks. Generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) revealed dynamic, non‐linear developmental trajectories that differed by proficiency and task type. Lower‐proficiency learners exhibited an inverted U‐shaped pattern in syntactic complexity, whereas higher‐proficiency learners showed stability in syntax but a non‐linear increase in lexical sophistication. Regarding task effects, debate tasks consistently elicited greater syntactic complexity than opinion‐gap tasks and showed an overall increase in lexical sophistication. LRE analysis indicated that learners focused primarily on lexis over grammar, with reliance on the L1 increasing over time. Pedagogically, these findings highlight the dynamic nature of language development in GenAI‐mediated interactions and suggest that AI‐based tasks should be designed considering learner proficiency and task type to maximize learning opportunities.

items.title: Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: As LLM agents increasingly execute complex, multi-step tasks on shared inference infrastructure, resource contention across the end-to-end LLM serving stack causes severe and uneven slowdowns across agents. Existing agentic serving systems primarily optimize throughput and latency, with comparatively limited attention to fairness among concurrent agents. Although fairness has been studied in conventional LLM serving at the token and request levels, these approaches do not fully capture cumulative delays and stateful resource dependencies across successive LLM calls within an agent. Moreover, interference spans request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware resources, making agent-level fairness challenging to define and optimize across an end-to-end serving stack. This paper presents a cross-layer framework to define agent-level fairness, attribute sources of unfairness, and optimize fairness while preserving throughput. To account for agents with widely varying execution demands, we build a theoretical foundation to define fairness using slowdown relative to standalone execution. Our empirical analysis reveals that routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention jointly determine fairness, with performance-oriented policies often leading to prolonged queuing delays. To optimize fairness, we introduce Duru, which monitors each agent's slowdown and uses this signal to guide admission and scheduling decisions across the router and runtime. Duru further alleviates starvation through admission exceptions and integrates slowdown-driven autoscaling to adhere to Service-Level Objectives (SLOs). Our evaluation across various benchmarks and hardware platforms shows that Duru reduces 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while delivering 91.8-127.4% of the state-of-the-art system's throughput.

items.title: Between risk and reform: Learning designers’ experiences of institutional responses to GenAI in assessment

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

items.abstract_text: Tomographic volumetric printing (TVP) is an emerging three-dimensional (3D) technique that enables rapid, layer-free fabrication of sophisticated structures via multi-angle light projection. While tomographic volumetric bioprinting (TVBP) extends to print with living cells, allowing for fast fabrication of cell-laden 3D constructs. This review summarizes recent algorithmic advances in TV(B)P, with emphasis on algorithmic strategies for improving printing resolution and fidelity, including optimization of light refraction, scattering, and iterative reconstruction. Then, we further explore increasing attention on the emergence of AI-based TV(B)P, enabling automatic parameter optimization, adaptive exposure control, accelerated slicing, and automated quality assessment. Further, we compare the differences between algorithm-based and AI-based strategies, as well as the difference between AI-driven TV(B)P, by which the system is granted autonomous decision-making power at critical stages of manufacturing; and AI-assisted TV(B)P, by which efficiency, robustness, and interpretability are enhanced without replacing existing physical or algorithmic models. items.abstract_text: Proprioceptive impairment is a common consequence of sports-related musculoskeletal injuries and is associated with altered neuromuscular control, impaired joint stability, delayed functional recovery, and an increased risk of reinjury. Conventional proprioceptive and sensorimotor assessments, including joint position sense testing, balance assessment, force-platform analysis, and isokinetic dynamometry, provide valuable clinical information, but they are often limited by laboratory dependence, intermittent measurement, cost, and reduced ecological validity. Wearable sensors, including inertial measurement units, pressure-sensing insoles, surface electromyography sensors, and sensor-integrated braces or smart textiles, provide portable quantitative measures of joint kinematics, postural control, gait, landing mechanics, and neuromuscular activation during functional tasks. This narrative review was informed by a structured, non-systematic literature search in PubMed, supplemented by targeted publisher searches and backward reference screening, updated through 31 August 2026, with an injury-focused PubMed update on 7 October 2026. English-language peer-reviewed studies and relevant reviews were prioritized, with direct evidence from sports-injury populations distinguished from indirect or transferable evidence from other populations. The review examines sensor modalities, their relationship to proprioceptive and broader sensorimotor outcomes, real-time biofeedback, home rehabilitation and remote monitoring, artificial intelligence-assisted analysis, and challenges in reliability, validity, and standardization. Current evidence supports technical feasibility and selected measurement and feedback applications, but many sensor-derived outcomes are influenced by pain, strength, fatigue, fear, attention, and compensatory strategies and should not be interpreted as direct measures of proprioceptive acuity. Evidence that wearable monitoring improves adherence, prevents reinjury, supports return-to-sport decisions, or enables clinically effective AI decision support remains limited. Clinical translation is further constrained by heterogeneous protocols, measurement error, limited external validation, small or selective datasets, privacy and usability concerns, and the absence of broadly accepted reference values. Future work should progress from analytical validation and reproducibility to prospective clinical validation, multicenter evaluation, and demonstration of athlete-relevant benefit.

This study examined a chain mediation model in which generative AI feedback use is associated with writing self-regulation through feedback literacy and, in turn, second language writing anxiety. The total indirect effect was 0.128 [0.094, 0.167], or 48.3% of the total association: 0.086 [0.053, 0.122] via feedback literacy, 0.024 [0.008, 0.049] via writing anxiety, and 0.018 [0.009, 0.031] for the serial route. Discussion These estimates describe associations rather than effects of an intervention. With no wave-1 baselines of anxiety or self-regulation and with two within-wave orderings resting on theory, the design cannot establish temporal sequence or within-person change. items.abstract_text: University students, particularly those who also work or hold organizational roles, frequently experience academic overload, stress, and burnout. Existing digital tools tend to address either task management or well-being, rarely both, and many lose users within days. This study reports the evidence-informed design of StudyFlow, a mobile-first platform that helps students turn unstructured academic demands into a prioritized, actionable plan, and examines how its design aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A design science research approach was followed. A targeted narrative review of literature published from 2021 to 2026 on student stress, working students, digital well-being interventions, engagement, and gamification informed a proto-persona, eight use cases, and nine functional requirements. A high-fidelity interactive prototype was generated through a five-stage natural-language prompt sequence in Google Stitch and refined in Google AI Studio. The intended feature set was compared with four widely used productivity and well-being applications, and each feature group was mapped to SDG targets with measurable evaluation indicators. The review yielded seven design implications, each traced to specific requirements and interface decisions. The prototype implements a four-stage workflow (set up, capture, organize and act, reflect) across dashboard, brain dump, task, focus, insights, and settings screens. None of the four comparator applications supported academic assignment breakdown, and none combined task capture, prioritization, focus support, reflection, and progress feedback in a single workflow. Streaks and usage metrics were deliberately framed as optional, non-punitive cues. StudyFlow shows how evidence on student stress and app engagement can be translated into a coherent, low-friction design that targets student well-being (SDG Target 3.4), persistence in tertiary education (Target 4.3), and the inclusion of working students (Target 10.2). Because no user testing has yet been conducted, no effectiveness claims are made; a staged usability and pilot evaluation protocol is proposed.

items.abstract_text: A polished assignment can conceal who chose the method, weighed the evidence and reached the conclusion, which makes a student’s independent reasoning difficult to assess. Drawing on the metacognitive account of cognitive offloading and Social Cognitive Theory, this qualitative study examined how reliance on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) relates to independent thinking, cognitive confidence and intellectual autonomy. Semi-structured online interviews were conducted with 22 undergraduate and postgraduate students, aged 20 to 29, from universities in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, each describing a recent academic episode involving GenAI. Thematic analysis traced when students sought assistance, which decisions they delegated and how they later justified their choices, and produced six themes. Delegating study planning preserved autonomy when students kept control over content, whereas removing a familiar AI prompt exposed difficulty in selecting a method despite earlier success with calculations. Confidence also diverged from accuracy: one student withheld a sound answer without AI confirmation, while another trusted a diagnosis because AI agreed with it, although both had missed the same error. Comparing drafts, checking sources and answering peers’ questions helped students identify assumptions and give reasons for revision. The findings support assessment practices that distinguish producing an answer with assistance from being able to explain or defend it without assistance.

items.abstract_text: Abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into workplaces is transforming not only how employees perform their tasks but also how they experience work. However, the implications of this transformation for sustainable development remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding whether AI-enabled workplaces can support employees’ long-term well-being and resilience. Addressing this gap, this study examines how positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT) and responsible AI signals (RAIS) contribute to multidimensional Green Well-being through employee engagement (ENG). Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Signaling Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources theory, Green Well-being is conceptualized as a sustainable state encompassing emotional (GEW), cognitive (GCW), and social well-being (GSW). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 342 knowledge workers employed by Vietnamese organizations using Generative AI. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that both POS_ATT (β = 0.312, p < 0.001) and RAIS (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) are positively associated with employee engagement. ENG, in turn, is positively associated with all three dimensions of Green Well-being, with the strongest relationship observed for emotional well-being (β = 0.441), followed by cognitive (β = 0.418) and social well-being (β = 0.397), all at p < 0.001. Moreover, ENG fully mediates the relationships between POS_ATT and RAIS and the three Green Well-being dimensions. These findings broaden understanding of sustainable development in AI-enabled workplaces by showing that the potential human benefits of Generative AI are not associated solely with technology adoption. Rather, favorable employee perceptions and responsible implementation need to be translated into meaningful work engagement before they are associated with sustainable well-being outcomes. The study therefore identifies responsible AI, employee engagement, and multidimensional well-being as interconnected elements of a human-centered approach to sustainable digital transformation. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Because the cross-sectional design captures relationships at a single point in time, the findings establish associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; responsible AI; employee engagement; Green Well-being; sustainable development; sustainable digital transformation.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

Assessment-Stratified Meta-Analysis

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Head-to-head within-AI trials (k = 6) favored pedagogical guardrails and teacher mediation over unguarded GenAI (g = +0.645 [+0.215, +1.075], p = .0033), whereas upper-secondary algebra and calculus cohorts showed acute offloading and workingmemory overload. Conclusions. Unstratified, unclustered synthesis inflates verified closed-resource mathematics learning by +0.26 to +0.29 SD (naive g = +0.275 vs. closed-resource g = −0.010). Durable competence requires crossing two distinct thresholds. Instructional systems must block direct answer copying and enforce active learner generation before and after AI withdrawal.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Secondary school students increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), and evidence shows it can either support or weaken their self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether teacher metacognitive scaffolding (TMS) and AI literacy (AIL) are related to SRL through productive cognitive offloading (PCO) and substitutive cognitive offloading (SCO), and whether peer collaborative AI use (PCAU) strengthens the link between scaffolding and productive offloading. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 327 students from 24 classes in eight Indonesian madrasah aliyah (Islamic senior high schools) selected through stratified multistage cluster sampling. We analysed the data using partial least squares structural equation modelling with 10,000 bootstrap subsamples. The measurement model met the reliability and validity criteria. TMS was positively related to PCO (β = 0.378) and negatively related to SCO (β = −0.351), and AIL showed the same pattern with smaller coefficients. PCO was positively related to SRL (β = 0.291), whereas SCO was negatively related to it (β = −0.266). Both forms of offloading partially mediated the relationships of TMS and AIL with SRL. PCAU strengthened the TMS–PCO path (β = 0.257), and scaffolding was not significantly related to productive offloading when peer collaboration was low. The model explained 45.8% of the variance in SRL. The findings indicate that teacher guidance is associated with SRL both directly and, for nearly half of its total effect, through the way students offload their thinking to GenAI, particularly when students verify AI outputs together.

items.title: Too good to resist? Affective engagement and a competence–regulation gap predict self-reported over-reliance on generative AI among vocational foreign-language learners

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors ( n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out ( β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment ( β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own ( r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially ( r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance ( β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance ( M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

items.title: Designing compassionate conversational AI: A preliminary Self Determination Theory framework for digital wellbeing

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Conversational Agents (CAs) is rapidly transforming higher education by providing personalised learning support, adaptive feedback, and interactive educational experiences. However, most research has focused on learning performance rather than students psychological wellbeing. This scoping review examines how Self-Determination Theory (SDT) has been applied in the design of conversational AI to promote digital wellbeing and compassionate educational technology. Guided by the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), a systematic search of four major databases identified 28 eligible studies published between 2018 and 2026. Thematic analysis revealed that conversational AI predominantly supports students competence through intelligent tutoring, adaptive scaffolding, and personalised feedback, while explicit support for autonomy and relatedness remains limited. Digital wellbeing is rarely considered an intended design outcome. Based on these findings, the review proposes a preliminary SDT informed conversational AI design framework comprising four interconnected principles which are supporting learner autonomy, strengthening competence, fostering relatedness through compassionate interactions, and promoting responsible AI use to enhance digital wellbeing. Integrating motivational psychology with human-centred AI design, this review provides practical guidance for developing AI systems that support learner agency, psychological wellbeing, and sustainable engagement, contributing to the design of compassionate educational technologies for the future of higher education.

items.title: When AI makes learning feel effortless: how processing fluency shapes students’ metacognitive judgments

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make learning feel easier, but whether this ease helps students accurately judge what they have learned remains unclear. Drawing on the cue-utilization framework, this research examines processing fluency as a metacognitive mechanism linking GenAI-assisted learning to judgments of learning (JOLs) and calibration. Across three experiments with university students, we tested how AI assistance, explanation fluency, and unaided retrieval shape subjective learning judgments relative to subsequent independent test performance. Study 1 ( N = 264) showed that GenAI-assisted learning increased processing fluency and JOLs, with a significant indirect association linking AI assistance to JOLs through processing fluency. Study 2 ( N = 360) manipulated fluency in scripted AI explanations delivered through a simulated GenAI interface and compared them with conventional-text learning. High-fluency explanations elicited higher JOLs and greater positive calibration bias than low-fluency explanations and conventional-text learning, although the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in objective test performance. Absolute calibration error did not differ significantly across conditions. Study 3 ( N = 386) showed that a brief no-AI retrieval attempt substantially weakened the relationship between processing fluency and JOL and reduced overall positive calibration bias. However, the retrieval-related reduction in calibration bias did not differ significantly between the high and low-fluency conditions. Together, the findings suggest that GenAI can shape metacognitive judgments by changing how fluent learning feels, while the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in immediate independent test performance. Providing learners with opportunities for unaided retrieval may help shift judgments from AI-generated processing ease toward more diagnostic evidence of what they can independently retrieve.

items.title: Beyond Operational Fluency: A Three-Tier AI Literacy Architecture for Reskilling and Upskilling in Strategic Talent Development
items.venue: International Journal of AI in Pedagogy Innovation and Learning Futures

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.title: AI usage, large language model dependence, and critical thinking among university students: the mediating roles of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into higher education has intensified debate over how AI-assisted learning may be associated with students’ cognitive development. Although prior studies have examined the benefits and risks of AI use, less attention has been paid to the distinction between frequent AI usage as a learning behavior and large language model dependence (LLMD) as a habitual reliance on LLMs for cognitive and academic tasks. This study therefore distinguishes frequent AI usage as a learning behavior from LLMD as a habitual reliance on LLMs when completing cognitive and academic tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined how AI usage is associated with university students’ critical thinking through LLMD, metacognitive awareness, and AI literacy. Survey data were collected from 878 Chinese university students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with LLMD, which represented the strongest direct association in the model, while LLMD was negatively associated with metacognitive awareness, AI literacy, and critical thinking. The mediation analysis further indicated a significant negative total indirect association between AI usage and critical thinking through LLMD and lower levels of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy. These findings contribute to the literature by clarifying the distinction between AI usage and LLMD and by identifying metacognitive awareness and AI literacy as cognitive resources associated with critical thinking in AI-assisted learning contexts. Practically, the study suggests that universities should move beyond simple restriction-oriented responses and pay greater attention to the quality of students’ AI engagement, including metacognitive monitoring, AI literacy, and awareness of dependence-related patterns.

items.title: AI as Psychological Surrogate in Consumer Search: A Conceptual Framework and Future Research Directions

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming ubiquitous in consumers' lives and search activities. AI applications that can create content, have conversations, respond to emotions, recognize images and objects, and construct real‐world experiences (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Google Lens, Apple Vision Pro) are transforming consumer search by functioning as psychological surrogates that assume key cognitive, evaluative, perceptual, and relational processes on consumers' behalf. Yet limited research has examined how these technologies transform the psychological mechanisms underlying consumer search. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic narrative review of 75 articles on the psychological foundations of consumer search and introduces the concept of AI psychological surrogacy, which happens when advanced‐AI technologies assume key psychological processes traditionally performed by humans. We develop a conceptual framework that theorizes AI psychological surrogacy across three higher‐order systems (affective‐relational delegation, cognitive‐evaluative substitution, and sensory‐perceptual construction) and six mechanisms: affective transference, relational surrogacy, cognitive delegation, evaluative surrogacy, perceptual offloading, and sensory augmentation. We advance six research propositions and a research agenda for investigating how reliance on AI as a psychological surrogate may alter consumer cognition, evaluation, perception, and relational dynamics.

items.abstract_text: Introduction: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can minimise large language model hallucinations while supporting self-regulated learning. We evaluated the impact of student engagement with a grounded RAG-AI tool (Google NotebookLM) on formative and internal assessment scores in undergraduate pathology, validated a 3-item AI Disclosure Form, and explored cognitive adoption barriers. Methods In a 12-week longitudinal study using an interrupted time series design, Phase II medical students (N = 211) received curated NotebookLM modules alongside core lectures. Students completed weekly quizzes, a 3-item disclosure form assessing the frequency, application mode, and trust in the AI resources, and end-of-study mixed-method questionnaires. Longitudinal cohorts were classified into High, Low, Inconsistent, and non-usage groups, with differences evaluated via ANOVA. Results The 3-item disclosure form demonstrated high reliability. The average scores of formative quizzes (p = 0.656) and summative internal exams (p = 0.961) did not differ significantly between the engagement groups. However, there were notable differences in performance during some of the dense, complex sections (Lung, p < 0.001; Renal, p < 0.001). Frequent users used active Socratic chat and self-quizzing to handle high cognitive demands. In contrast, inconsistent users showed "cognitive flight" under stress, and non-respondents scored significantly lower (24.83 ± 13.76). Conclusion A standalone RAG-AI tool does not automatically improve the overall performance of a group. Instead, it helps manage cognitive load during demanding modules for learners who are good at self-regulated learning. Future use needs structured workflows within a Learning Management System and training for prompt verification.

items.abstract_text: This study examined the effects of Generative AI (GenAI)-assisted learning on the critical thinking skills of higher secondary school students. A quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test design with a non-equivalent control group was used. The sample consisted of 59 Grade XII students of Garrison Academy Kharian Cantt (Army Public School and College), Punjab, Pakistan: 28 girls in the experimental group and 31 boys in the control group. For one month, the experimental group was taught with GenAI tools (Claude and DeepSeek) and the control group was taught with traditional methods. Critical thinking was measured before and after the teaching period with a 30-item Critical Thinking Questionnaire based on Facione's (1990) six skills: interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, and self-regulation. The data were analysed with paired-samples t-tests, independent-samples t-tests on gain scores, and analysis of covariance. The total critical thinking score of the experimental group rose from M = 72.71 (SD = 5.11) to M = 121.25 (SD = 7.79), t(27) = 29.02, p < .001, d = 7.37, and that of the control group rose from M = 68.68 (SD = 7.75) to M = 77.58 (SD = 8.03), t(30) = 8.15, p < .001, d = 1.13. The mean gain of the experimental group (48.54 points) was significantly larger than that of the control group (8.90 points), t(57) = 20.21, p < .001, d = 5.27, and the analysis of covariance, which adjusted for the pre-test score, gave the same result, F(1, 56) = 466.24, p < .001, partial η² = .893. All six skills improved more in the experimental group. For classroom practice, the result suggests that guided GenAI activities, in which students compare AI answers, check them against the textbook, and give their own reasons, are worth adding to regular teaching under the teacher's supervision. The effect sizes were unusually large, the experimental group also started higher than the control group (p = .023), and the pre-test reliability of the questionnaire was low (α = .29). The findings should be read with care because the groups were intact classes that also differed in gender. Keywords: Generative AI, Critical Thinking Skills, Higher Secondary Students, Quasi-Experimental Study

items.title: Human-first learning: scaffolding reasoning before AI assistance improves diagnostic accuracy

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative AI could improve physicians' clinical performance, yet its use in medical training raises questions about whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use AI effectively and independently. We conducted a longitudinal randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students (389 analysed). Students completed clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were randomised to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the AI assistant, the AI assistant followed by scaffolding, or both simultaneously. AI scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their reasoning without providing direct answers; the assistant provided requested information and answers. The study comprised an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn. Frontier large language models (LLMs) completed the same tasks as an additional benchmark. Students initially performed below LLMs but later exceeded them following the interventions. Students who began with AI scaffolding achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than those given access to the AI assistant from the outset both during the subsequent intervention phase (75.2% vs 66.0%; OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12–2.68]) and after withdrawal (24.6% vs 14.4%; OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15–4.14]). After withdrawal, scaffold-first groups were the only groups to outperform both unsupported students (24.5–24.7% vs 9.0%; ORs 3.77–3.87, 95% CIs [1.25–12.00]) and LLMs (24.5–24.7% vs 8.6%; ORs 3.48–3.50, 95% CIs [1.22–9.89]). Introducing the AI assistant after scaffolding decreased intrinsic cognitive load ( t (50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and increased metacognitive evaluation ( t (50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). These findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding precedes answer-providing assistance to strengthen diagnostic performance both during AI-supported learning and after AI support is withdrawn.

items.title: Generative AI Use and Student Well-Being in Higher Education: A Literature Review
items.venue: Academic journal of management and social sciences

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning practices, yet its implications for student well-being remain insufficiently explored. This literature review synthesizes existing evidence on the potential benefits and risks of generative AI use for university student well-being and examines the psychological mechanisms that may explain these relationships. The reviewed literature suggests that when generative AI is used as a learning-support tool, it may contribute to reduced academic stress, stronger learning confidence, greater learning efficiency, emotional support, and greater satisfaction with task completion. In contrast, when AI substitutes for rather than supports core cognitive processes, its use may be associated with over-reliance, diminished autonomous learning, academic-integrity concerns, AI-related employment anxiety, and technostress. Self-efficacy, cognitive offloading, academic stress, and autonomy emerge as important psychological mechanisms through which generative AI use may relate to student well-being. Overall, the relationship between generative AI use and student well-being does not appear to be uniformly beneficial or harmful but varies according to how, why, and to what extent students use AI. Future research should therefore move beyond whether students use generative AI and examine more precisely the patterns and conditions of use that support or undermine student well-being.

items.abstract_text: AI is only the latest in a succession of educational technologies that have made learning easier and more frictionless, which, counterintuitively, has coincided with a population-level decline in cognitive ability and poor learning outcomes. Studies in cognitive offloading and productive struggle suggest it may be affordances of information technology exacerbated by AI that contribute to these poor outcomes. Describing the relevance of cognitive offloading, cognitive load theory and the expertise reversal effect, this paper explores the cognitive mechanisms associated with technological assistance that have been shown to affect learning, and considers pathways to redesign learning in a way that focuses on useful forms of learning friction, understood as the effortful work that consolidates learning. The paper locates these cognitive mechanisms near the learner experience where self-regulation holds the most potential to effect change when combined with educator support. The question for educators, designers and students will continue to evolve: does experiencing friction enhance learning? A heuristic is offered as a conceptual model of a process for teachers and designers to support learners at the point where cognitive offloading occurs.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This review synthesizes evidence from recent studies of human–AI collaboration in service and digital ecosystems to build and test a multi-level conceptual framework. Design/methodology/approach: Thirteen studies (Tier A) from 2024 to 2026 were analyzed in full text and compared with 25 qualitative and mixed-methods studies (Tier B). In total, 38 service and digital ecosystem studies were analyzed within this review. Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and the Affect–Behavior–Cognition (ABC) model was used as the underlying theoretical framework. Narrative and thematic analysis were employed to synthesize the results from the included studies. Findings: Transparency, process control and outcome control have significant effects on employees in terms of cognitive and behavioral effects, while system-initiated engagement has little effect. Human–AI interaction does not, on average, perform better than the best human in each task (g = ?0.23, p < .001), but does perform better than a single human in a variety of tasks (g = 0.64). Value is created through the integration of systems and not through technology itself. User experience, digital maturity, interoperable IT, and AI-induced technostress condition value realization. Originality/value: The study provides a three-stage framework, seven testable hypotheses, seven gaps in current research and an operational measurement for value creation at the employee level and for firm- and network-level value co-creation.

items.abstract_text: Purpose The integration of artificial intelligence with Lean construction has been shown to promote added value and drive growth in the built environment. However, understanding of their interaction across multiple levels of abstraction remains limited, especially beyond technical optimisation. This article systematically reviews the interaction between AI and Lean construction to identify current interactions, major applications and research gaps. Design/methodology/approach Following the PRISMA protocol, 63 peer-reviewed studies were identified and analysed qualitatively. AI techniques were mapped against Lean construction principles, waste categories and Lean methods to enable a multi-level comparative synthesis. Findings The results show a growing interest over the past four years, with a focus on AI techniques such as machine learning, optimisation and computer vision used to enhance workflow and to reduce cycle times, particularly within the Last Planner System. Nonetheless, principles centred on value creation, collaboration and partner development remain largely underexplored. Similarly, a co-adaptive relationship was observed to be emerging, in which AI improves Lean's technical efficiency while Lean principles guide AI's development towards ethical and value-driven outcomes. Research limitations/implications The findings offer a foundation for advancing Lean Construction 4.0 through socio-technical integration and human-centred innovation. Practitioners can start by applying mature AI techniques to improve measurable Lean outcomes such as workflow reliability, constraint prediction, visual management and waste reduction, then extend GenAI and NLP tools to collaboration, requirement capture, knowledge reuse and cross-project learning. Originality/value The study proposes a dual-focus model that separates AI's current role as a technical enabler from its future potential as a holistic partner.

items.abstract_text: This convergent mixed-methods multiple-case study examined how 16 Indonesian EFL undergraduates exercised revision agency while using generative-AI feedback across four connected writing tasks. The corpus comprised 64 final texts, 48.5 hours of screen recording, 342 prompt-response decision episodes, 16 interviews, stimulated recall, four focus-group reflections, and a 96-page analytic memo trail. Descriptive episode coding identified four patterns: selective scaffolding (38.6%), iterative co-composition (29.2%), surface repair (21.3%), and delegated composition (10.8%). Integrated qualitative analysis showed that high-agency use was marked by a bounded purpose, comparison of alternatives, transformation or rejection of output, verification, and the ability to defend the final text. High-proficiency students most often used selective scaffolding and rejected about 65% of outputs; intermediate students more often negotiated through iterative co-composition and rejected about 35%; low-intermediate students more often relied on surface repair or delegation and rejected about 10%. Frequency of AI use was therefore a weak indicator of learning or responsibility. Revision agency depended on what students did between receiving feedback and submitting text. The study contributes a process-based taxonomy and an evidence model for distinguishing assistance from substitution. It recommends bounded prompting, accept-modify-reject rationales, verification routines, teacher moderation, revision memos, and independent performance evidence.

items.abstract_text: This study investigates whether LLM-based Conversational Agents (LLMCAs) could be employed as assistive technologies, helping anyone navigate a website by explaining its content and interactive features, and suggesting actions to accomplish specific goals. This would make the web more accessible especially to seniors, blind users and people with mild cognitive impairment. Specifically, the study examines whether such tools can analyze the source code of a webpage to identify its structure and interactive elements, understand which interactive components are required to support users in achieving their goals, and act effectively as assistive technologies. In addition, the work compares leading tools to assess differences in their effectiveness and behavior in supporting accessible web interaction. The work presents two empirical studies in which four popular LLMCA tools are evaluated on a set of public websites, in order to assess their ability to understand web page structures and interactive components and assist users in their tasks. The evaluation combines qualitative and quantitative measures, focusing on accuracy, completeness, and practical usefulness of the responses.Results show a good degree of pertinent and good-quality answers, even on websites with a poorly accessible structure. The user-friendly way to interact with a LLMCA makes it much comfortable to use for the average user. However, the study also highlights that some LLMCAs appear more 'skilled' in accessibility tasks than others. LLMCAs show promising potential not only to complement existing assistive technologies but also to support or replace the human assistance that is often required for many users to effectively access the web.

items.abstract_text: This study examines prompt literacy among future computer science teachers in the context of solving and debugging programming tasks with ChatGPT. It focuses on students' perceptions of prompt literacy, their understanding of responsible AI use, documented practices of verifying and modifying AI-assisted solutions, and patterns of academic performance. A descriptive multi-method study was conducted during a 16-week programming course involving 113 future computer science teachers at Kh. Dosmukhamedov Atyrau University, Kazakhstan. Data were collected through questionnaires, student programming submissions, ChatGPT-use disclosure notes, reflective comments, code-similarity screening, and course-grade records. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative content analysis was used to identify recurring patterns in students' reported use, verification, and revision of AI-generated solutions. The findings were compared across data sources to address the research questions without testing causal effects or participant-level associations. The 20-item Prompt-Literacy Perceptions Questionnaire demonstrated high overall internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.94). Students generally reported positive perceptions of ChatGPT for code generation, debugging, and explaining programming logic. They also recognized the importance of verifying AI-generated outputs and disclosing substantial AI assistance. However, students' documentation of verification and modification practices was frequently general rather than detailed. Pairwise code-similarity screening identified relatively few submission pairs exceeding the predefined 50% similarity threshold. Mean academic scores were numerically close across practical assignments and independent control tasks, although differences in assessment conditions and grading criteria limited direct comparisons. The findings highlight the importance of integrating prompt literacy, critical verification, and transparent documentation of AI use into computer science teacher education. Positive perceptions of responsible ChatGPT use did not necessarily correspond to detailed documentation of verification and revision practices. Code-similarity results cannot independently establish whether students modified AI-generated solutions. Furthermore, the descriptive single-cohort design does not support conclusions about causal effects or improvements in prompt-literacy competence. The study emphasizes the pedagogical value of making students' reasoning, verification, and responsible AI-use practices explicit during programming instruction.

items.abstract_text: Drawing on dynamic usage‐based and interactionist SLA perspectives, this study investigated developmental patterns of linguistic complexity and language‐related episodes (LREs) during L2 learners' written interactions with ChatGPT. Ten Korean EFL learners completed seven sessions of opinion‐gap and debate tasks over 5 weeks. Generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) revealed dynamic, non‐linear developmental trajectories that differed by proficiency and task type. Lower‐proficiency learners exhibited an inverted U‐shaped pattern in syntactic complexity, whereas higher‐proficiency learners showed stability in syntax but a non‐linear increase in lexical sophistication. Regarding task effects, debate tasks consistently elicited greater syntactic complexity than opinion‐gap tasks and showed an overall increase in lexical sophistication. LRE analysis indicated that learners focused primarily on lexis over grammar, with reliance on the L1 increasing over time. Pedagogically, these findings highlight the dynamic nature of language development in GenAI‐mediated interactions and suggest that AI‐based tasks should be designed considering learner proficiency and task type to maximize learning opportunities.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

items.abstract_text: Tomographic volumetric printing (TVP) is an emerging three-dimensional (3D) technique that enables rapid, layer-free fabrication of sophisticated structures via multi-angle light projection. While tomographic volumetric bioprinting (TVBP) extends to print with living cells, allowing for fast fabrication of cell-laden 3D constructs. Our continuous work and the rapid developments on TVP/TVBP (TV(B)P) encourage us to review the current challenges faced by TV(B)P and the recent trend in algorithm-based optimization vs AI-based optimization. This review summarizes recent algorithmic advances in TV(B)P, with emphasis on algorithmic strategies for improving printing resolution and fidelity, including optimization of light refraction, scattering, and iterative reconstruction. Then, we further explore increasing attention on the emergence of AI-based TV(B)P, enabling automatic parameter optimization, adaptive exposure control, accelerated slicing, and automated quality assessment. Further, we compare the differences between algorithm-based and AI-based strategies, as well as the difference between AI-driven TV(B)P, by which the system is granted autonomous decision-making power at critical stages of manufacturing; and AI-assisted TV(B)P, by which efficiency, robustness, and interpretability are enhanced without replacing existing physical or algorithmic models. In summary, this review offers insights into the future directions of AI-based TV(B)P in materials science, biomedical engineering, and advanced manufacturing.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence has introduced a new communicative environment in which users formulate language for an artificial conversational partner rather than exclusively for another human being. This development raises important sociolinguistic questions about how multilingual speakers modify their language when they perceive particular communicative requirements from an AI system. The present study develops a corpus-informed investigation of communication accommodation among Brahui-speaking Pakistani university students interacting with ChatGPT. Drawing on Communication Accommodation Theory (CAT), the study examines how students adjust lexical, structural, pragmatic, and language-choice practices during human–AI interaction. A mixed-methods, corpus-assisted discourse analysis design is proposed, combining approximately 100–150 student–ChatGPT interaction sequences from 50–80 Brahui-speaking university students with a language-background questionnaire and follow-up semi-structured interviews with 15 participants. The interaction corpus will be examined through frequency, concordance, collocation, code-switching, and qualitative discourse analysis using AntConc and, where available, Sketch Engine. Interview data will be thematically analyzed using NVivo. The analytical framework distinguishes convergence, divergence, maintenance, interpretability-oriented accommodation, and repair. Particular attention is given to the relationship among Brahui, Urdu, and English and to the possibility that students perceive English as more compatible with AI-mediated academic communication. Because the empirical corpus and interviews have not yet been collected, illustrative interactional examples in this manuscript are explicitly fictional and are included only to demonstrate the proposed analytical procedures. The study is designed to extend CAT into multilingual human–AI communication and to foreground the experiences of speakers of an indigenous/minoritized language in Pakistan. It further considers the implications of AI-mediated communication for linguistic identity, digital inclusion, multilingual education, and the visibility of Brahui in emerging AI environments. publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Proprioceptive impairment is a common consequence of sports-related musculoskeletal injuries and is associated with altered neuromuscular control, impaired joint stability, delayed functional recovery, and an increased risk of reinjury. Conventional proprioceptive and sensorimotor assessments, including joint position sense testing, balance assessment, force-platform analysis, and isokinetic dynamometry, provide valuable clinical information, but they are often limited by laboratory dependence, intermittent measurement, cost, and reduced ecological validity. Wearable sensors, including inertial measurement units, pressure-sensing insoles, surface electromyography sensors, and sensor-integrated braces or smart textiles, provide portable quantitative measures of joint kinematics, postural control, gait, landing mechanics, and neuromuscular activation during functional tasks. This narrative review was informed by a structured, non-systematic literature search in PubMed, supplemented by targeted publisher searches and backward reference screening, updated through 31 August 2026, with an injury-focused PubMed update on 7 October 2026. English-language peer-reviewed studies and relevant reviews were prioritized, with direct evidence from sports-injury populations distinguished from indirect or transferable evidence from other populations. The review examines sensor modalities, their relationship to proprioceptive and broader sensorimotor outcomes, real-time biofeedback, home rehabilitation and remote monitoring, artificial intelligence-assisted analysis, and challenges in reliability, validity, and standardization. Current evidence supports technical feasibility and selected measurement and feedback applications, but many sensor-derived outcomes are influenced by pain, strength, fatigue, fear, attention, and compensatory strategies and should not be interpreted as direct measures of proprioceptive acuity. Evidence that wearable monitoring improves adherence, prevents reinjury, supports return-to-sport decisions, or enables clinically effective AI decision support remains limited. Clinical translation is further constrained by heterogeneous protocols, measurement error, limited external validation, small or selective datasets, privacy and usability concerns, and the absence of broadly accepted reference values. Future work should progress from analytical validation and reproducibility to prospective clinical validation, multicenter evaluation, and demonstration of athlete-relevant benefit.
