items.abstract_text: Connectivity programmes often assume that a young person who gets online will be able to find a way to earn. Evidence provides partial support: faster internet has increased employment in a number of African countries [17]. However, many young Africans with internet access continue to work in informal, low-paid and insecure jobs. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) raises a further question: who is able to benefit from these technologies, and under what conditions might they widen existing disparities? This paper asks what needs to connect digital access to sustainable livelihoods for young people in Kenya and, by implication, in other African contexts. It develops the Capability-to-Livelihood Pathway Framework, comprising five interrelated components: access conditions; a four-level capability stack connecting foundational digital literacy, functional AI literacy, critical AI literacy and occupational application; conversion factors that shape whether capabilities can generate income; livelihood pathways; and outcome measures focused on security and progression rather than income at a single point in time. The framework is developed through an integrative conceptual synthesis of scholarship on digital inequality, AI and employment, youth employment programmes, and relevant policy and labour-market evidence, using Kenya as the principal contextual case. Four propositions are advanced for empirical testing. The paper’s central contribution is to shift the measure of programme success from skills delivered to livelihoods sustained.

items.abstract_text: This conceptual paper examines AI-enabled smart retailing as a customer-facing service transformation in Internet commerce rather than as a narrow technological or operational innovation. Drawing on a selective, theory-driven synthesis of services marketing, smart retailing, AI-enabled marketing, customer experience, service-dominant logic, human–AI interaction, and responsible-AI research, it develops a three-layer framework linking AI-enabled service capabilities, customer-experience mechanisms, and Internet-commerce outcomes. The framework identifies three capability groups—algorithmic personalisation and decision support, AI-mediated service interaction, and predictive service intelligence—and four evaluative mechanisms: decision value, interaction quality, transaction confidence, and algorithmic legitimacy. These mechanisms shape customer satisfaction, engagement, service-recovery effectiveness, platform trust, relationship quality, continuance intention, value co-creation, and inclusive service value. Human–AI governance, including privacy protection, transparency, fairness, customer control, human review, and digital accessibility, is treated as a boundary condition that determines whether AI-enabled services are perceived as trustworthy and customer-centred or as intrusive, opaque, unfair, and exclusionary. The paper contributes to Internet-commerce research by repositioning AI as a service-enabling capability and by explaining how customer evaluations translate AI applications into commercial and relational outcomes. It also proposes a focused research agenda for empirical testing across e-commerce websites, mobile applications, online marketplaces, social-commerce platforms, and omnichannel systems.

items.abstract_text: Chronic diseases are a major global public health concern and place a substantial burden on individuals, healthcare systems, and society. Their prevention and management depend not only on effective medical treatment but also on sustained engagement in health-promoting behaviors. These behaviors include regular physical activity, healthy dietary practices, medication adherence, self-monitoring, smoking cessation, and other disease-related self-management activities. However, initiating and maintaining such behaviors can be challenging, particularly because individuals differ in their health conditions, risk profiles, knowledge, motivation, behavioral readiness, and support needs. Therefore, accessible, personalized, and continuous interventions are needed to support health behavior change in both individuals at increased risk of chronic diseases and those already living with chronic conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents have emerged as promising tools for supporting health behavior change. Through natural language interaction and other interactive functions, these agents may provide personalized health information, motivational support, goal setting, action planning, self-monitoring, feedback, reminders, and ongoing behavioral guidance. Advances in natural language processing, machine learning, and large language models have further expanded the potential capabilities of AI agents, enabling more flexible, context-sensitive, and personalized interactions. Nevertheless, the application of AI agents in chronic disease prevention and management is developing rapidly, and the available evidence remains diverse in terms of target populations, technological approaches, intervention strategies, theoretical foundations, and evaluated outcomes. A comprehensive mapping of this evidence is needed to understand the current state of the field and identify priorities for future research and development. This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on the application of AI agents for health behavior change in chronic disease prevention and management. Specifically, it will examine the characteristics of the populations and chronic diseases addressed, the types and technological features of AI agents, the health behaviors targeted, the design and delivery of interventions, the behavioral theories and behavior change techniques employed, and the outcomes reported. Particular attention will be paid to how AI agents support behavior change through interactive communication, personalization, behavioral monitoring, feedback, motivational strategies, and other intervention components. The review will be guided by the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. The population will include individuals living with chronic diseases and those at increased risk of developing chronic diseases. The concept will focus on AI agents that provide interactive communication and behavioral support, including AI-powered chatbots, large language model-based agents, virtual health assistants, virtual coaches, dialogue systems, and other relevant interactive AI systems. The context will encompass chronic disease prevention and management across healthcare, community, home-based, and digital health settings. A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in nine electronic databases: China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data Knowledge Service Platform, China Science and Technology Journal Database (VIP), Chinese Biomedical Literature Database (SinoMed), PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, ProQuest, and Embase. The search strategy will combine terms related to artificial intelligence agents, chronic diseases, and health behavior change. Studies published in English or Chinese will be considered, with no restrictions on publication year. Reference lists of included studies and relevant review articles will also be screened to identify additional eligible publications. Eligible studies will include original empirical research investigating AI agents designed to promote, improve, or maintain health behaviors relevant to chronic disease prevention or management. A broad range of study designs will be considered, including randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, observational studies, qualitative studies, mixed-methods studies, pilot studies, and feasibility studies. Studies focusing exclusively on disease diagnosis, risk prediction, clinical decision support, or static health information provision without an identifiable behavioral intervention component will be excluded. The review will characterize the distribution of studies across publication years, countries, disease categories, AI agent types, and behavioral targets. It will also examine the relationships between AI agent capabilities, intervention strategies, and reported health behavior outcomes. items.title: Exploring multimodal AI--XR interactions for software development: From expert perspectives to semantic code outlines

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

items.abstract_text: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

items.abstract_text: This dataset comes from a nonequivalent control group pretest–posttest quasi-experiment conducted in a primary school in City S, Henan Province, China. Participants were 136 fourth-grade students (aged 9–11 years; 66 boys, 70 girls) from three intact parallel classes, assigned to conventional IPBL (n = 45), GenAI-supported IPBL (IPBL-GenAI, n = 47), or IPBL co-supported by the GenAI tool and teacher scaffolding (IPBL-GenAI-TS, n = 44). The study comprised five sessions: a uniform pre-test (Session 1), platform-orientation training (Session 2), the core intervention (Sessions 3–4, with the same instructor, the same project topic, and differentiated treatment across groups), and a parallel post-test after project completion (Session 5).The dataset contains three sheets: (1) learning motivation data (adapted from the elementary-school MUSIC Inventory; 12 items, 4-point scale, 4 dimensions: empowerment, usefulness, success, interest); (2) interdisciplinary problem-solving competence data (self-developed with reference to Tan et al.'s problem-solving assessment dimensions; 17 items, 5-point Likert scale, 3 dimensions: problem inquiry, problem representation, strategy execution with process regulation); and (3) a codebook with variable definitions and coding. items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and digital transformation are reshaping occupational tasks and challenging conventional models of career and technical education (CTE). This conceptual article argues that CTE should be reconceptualized from an educational pathway to workforce infrastructure that continuously connects education, industry, technology, policy, and lifelong learning. Drawing on the contrasting institutional contexts of the United States and China, the article examines how decentralization, systemic coordination, industry-education integration, apprenticeship, technological transformation, and continuing skill development shape national workforce capacity. It proposes a conceptual model of CTE as workforce infrastructure organized around five interconnected functions and four outcomes: occupational competence, human agency, workforce adaptability, and economic and social mobility. Five propositions explain relationships among institutional articulation, AI augmentation, transferable human capabilities, lifelong learning, and equitable access. items.abstract_text: AI-enabled medicine does not express a single anthropology, and digital health is not intrinsically transhumanist. Some platformised health arrangements nevertheless stabilise optimisation drift: a transition in which bounded aims of support, prevention, or capability preservation are progressively recoded as an open-ended duty of measurable correction. The drift becomes structurally closer to transhumanist perfectionism than to bounded enhancement when three properties converge: principled stopping rules lose practical force, embodiment is governed as an indefinitely corrigible substrate, and selective interventions escalate into a recursively expanding package of optimisation. Platform incentives, preventive rationalisation, and organisational pressures explain the emergence and diffusion of this pattern more directly than transhumanist doctrine; structural affinity identifies the normative grammar enacted once those properties converge. A reconstructive prohumanist framework evaluates that grammar through dignified longevity, understood as technologically supported continuation of life that preserves embodied agency, plural goods, recognition, justice, and meaningful exit. Four constraints follow: proportionality, contestability, non-totalisation, and epistemic autonomy. Applied to remote patient monitoring and episodic diagnostic AI, they distinguish bounded support from optimisation-by-default across design, deployment, review, and withdrawal.

items.abstract_text: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

items.abstract_text: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.

items.abstract_text: The study uses a Christian-anthropological approach to evaluate the educational application of generative artificial intelligence. Its central question is: what gives the teacher a human, irreplaceable essence, and which tasks can be delegated to artificial intelligence in ways that preserve the goals of Christian education while making learning more effective? The argument connects theological anthropology, personalist thinking, and educational research. As a conceptual-normative synthesis rather than an empirical intervention, it draws on the doctrine of Imago Dei, Buber’s I–Thou relation, and Simone Weil’s notion of attention to mark the ontological difference between the person and machine simulation. The article argues that artificial intelligence can significantly strengthen technical and informational pedagogical work, but it cannot replace the relational, moral, spiritual, and vocational dimensions of education. Functional similarity, on this reading, does not amount to substantial identity: a language model has no conscious self that could answer for its outputs. Learning understood as formatio also demands effort, waiting, and uncertainty, which the promise of frictionless learning tends to erase. Five dimensions of the teaching role – presence, moral responsibility, authority, vocational guidance, and community – are shown to resist automation. The study proposes a three-zone delegation matrix: delegable tasks, co-pilot tasks under teacher supervision, and non-delegable, person-specific pedagogical moments. Each zone is paired with its main risk and a pedagogical condition: factual error calls for teacher control and source criticism, deskilling for the teacher’s final decision, and depersonalization for a personal, accountable human judgment. The article concludes that the role of artificial intelligence in Christian education lies in multiplying human capabilities rather than replacing the human teacher.

Accordingly, the framework should be interpreted as a set of mechanism-based propositions rather than a validated causal model linking AI use directly to employability or employment. Because source identification and selection were purposive rather than exhaustive, the conclusions remain subject to selection and publication bias, geographical imbalance, methodological heterogeneity, reviewer judgment, and the rapid evolution of AI technologies. Of the 46 sources, 15 are classified as primary empirical publications, and four provide RQ1-specific direct evidence on AI-supported English-language learning. Two primary empirical publications examine graduate employability-related competencies or perceptions; one additional publication synthesizes earlier empirical assessments. items.abstract_text: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of large language models (LLMs) into intellectual activities requires a reconsideration of prompt engineering as more than the technical optimization of instructions. Although conventional prompting techniques primarily seek to improve the relevance, accuracy, and structure of artificial intelligence outputs, they often provide insufficient attention to the cognitive processes through which users formulate requests, evaluate generated information, regulate reliance on automation, and maintain independent judgment. This paper introduces Metacognitive Prompt Engineering (MPE) as a proposed human-centered framework for designing, monitoring, and regulating interactions with generative artificial intelligence. Drawing on theories of metacognition, self-regulated learning, cognitive monitoring, automation reliance, and human–AI collaboration, MPE conceptualizes prompting as an iterative process involving goal clarification, cognitive task allocation, epistemic monitoring, evidence-based verification, and adaptive strategy regulation. The paper distinguishes metacognitive prompt engineering from conventional prompt optimization and model-centered metacognitive prompting. It proposes a five-phase regulatory framework, identifies practical design principles, introduces reusable prompting protocols, and develops a research agenda for evaluating the framework's potential effects on cognitive autonomy, confidence calibration, decision quality, and independent learning. Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between model-generated expressions of uncertainty and independently justified confidence, as well as the limitations of self-correction without external feedback. The central argument is that effective human–AI interaction should be assessed not exclusively through the quality of generated outputs but also through the quality of the cognitive regulation exercised by the human user. MPE is presented as a theoretical and methodological proposal rather than an empirically validated intervention. Its effectiveness, boundary conditions, and possible unintended consequences require systematic investigation

items.abstract_text: Nearly a century of focused behavioral sciences research has attempted to tackle widespread behavioral challenges, including insufficient levels of physical activity, poor quality eating patterns, poor adherence to medical regimens, and more. Behavioral scientists are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI)-based technologies to advance the study of behavioral sciences, extend the precision and reach of their programs, and improve their ability to intervene at key moments. There are also new challenges associated with AI technologies, including a discrepancy between the speed of technological development and that of scientific process, ethical and environmental concerns, and the need to ensure that AI-enabled tools are appropriate, accessible, and attractive to diverse older adult users. At this early stage, it is critical that experts from diverse and relevant fields provide their perspectives on opportunities and challenges in the implementation of AI for guiding behavior change in older adults. To this end, the National Institute on Aging Research Centers Collaborative Network hosted a workshop, where a various body of scientific and clinical experts discussed opportunities and challenges regarding the use of AI in behavior change interventions for older adults. We summarize this discussion, highlighting both opportunities and challenges, and present several key areas for future research.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and teacher self-efficacy: from technology adoption to AI-mediated efficacy reconstruction

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in educational practice, transforming lesson planning, instructional delivery, assessment, learning analytics, and teacher professional development. Although research on AI in education has expanded rapidly, the psychological consequences of AI adoption for teachers remain theoretically fragmented. Existing studies have examined technology acceptance, AI literacy, technology self-efficacy, instructional confidence, and professional identity, yet these constructs have rarely been integrated into a coherent account of how AI reshapes teachers’ beliefs about their own professional capabilities. This narrative review synthesizes the emerging literature through a theory-building perspective grounded primarily in social cognitive theory and informed by technology acceptance, cognitive load, professional identity, social comparison, and human–AI interaction perspectives. We propose a framework of AI-Mediated Efficacy Reconstruction, conceptualizing AI not as a direct determinant of teacher self-efficacy but as a socio-technical factor that changes the availability, interpretation, and attribution of efficacy-relevant experiences. AI can facilitate mastery experiences, provide vicarious learning opportunities, offer timely feedback, reduce routine cognitive demands, and expand access to professional learning. However, the same technologies may generate cognitive overload, technical anxiety, professional comparison, identity threat, reduced autonomy, and technological dependence. We identify Efficacy Attribution as a potentially central mechanism determining whether AI-supported performance is internalized as evidence of teachers’ own professional capability or attributed primarily to the technological system. On this basis, we distinguish Augmented Efficacy, in which AI extends teachers’ capabilities while preserving professional agency, from Dependent Efficacy, in which perceived competence becomes increasingly contingent upon AI assistance. The framework further proposes that these processes are moderated by teacher characteristics, AI-system characteristics, teaching tasks, organizational context, and time. We conclude by outlining implications for measurement, teacher professional development, AI design, organizational policy, and future longitudinal and experimental research.

items.abstract_text: Enterprise application modernization has become an essential requirement for organizations seeking to improve operational efficiency, scalability, flexibility, and infrastructure utilization in rapidly evolving digital environments. Traditional enterprise applications frequently depend on monolithic architectures, tightly coupled services, and infrastructure-specific configurations that restrict deployment flexibility and increase maintenance complexity. This research proposes an integrated modernization framework combining serverless computing and Kubernetes-based cloud workload portability to improve enterprise application deployment and management. The proposed approach uses microservices architecture, containerization, serverless execution models, automated orchestration, and cloud-native deployment mechanisms to support flexible application execution across public, private, hybrid, and multi-cloud infrastructures. Kubernetes provides container orchestration, service discovery, workload scheduling, scaling, and application lifecycle management, while serverless computing enables event-driven execution and automatic resource allocation based on application demand. The framework incorporates automated deployment pipelines, infrastructure abstraction, API integration, workload monitoring, and resource optimization mechanisms. The research methodology focuses on architectural design, application containerization, serverless function integration, Kubernetes orchestration, and experimental performance evaluation. Key evaluation parameters include application response time, deployment efficiency, resource utilization, workload portability, scalability, and operational cost. The proposed framework aims to reduce infrastructure dependency, improve application availability, simplify modernization activities, and support consistent workload execution across heterogeneous cloud environments, providing enterprises with a flexible foundation for sustainable digital transformation.

items.abstract_text: Purpose There is a close association between the fast acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the rise in the time spent on screens by Generation Z students on a daily basis. Previous studies have focused on AI literacy as a facilitator of AI adoption and utilization. This paper attempts to find out whether AI literacy, self-regulation, digital wellbeing literacy, academic productivity, and FoMO predict students’ willingness to reduce digital habits through mindful technology use, moderated by digital self-efficacy and peer influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained through survey from 556 Generation Z college students and analysed using PLS-SEM. The measurement model was examined in terms of reliability and validity, the structural model was tested for direct, mediation and moderation effect, while the predictive relevance was estimated via a blindfolding approach. The results were validated using ANN analysis and fsQCA. Findings All five antecedents were found to be significant predictors of mindful technology usage in the hypothesized direction, and mindful technology use was a significant predictor of digital wellness and hence acted as a partial mediator of the five relationships. AI literacy was uniquely significant as a predictor of digital wellness. Digital self-efficacy selectively moderated only AI literacy and self-regulation paths, whereas peer influence did not moderate the relationship between mindful technology usage and digital wellness. The results from ANN highlighted the non-linear significance of digital well-being awareness and AI literacy, while fsQCA identified three equifinal combinations that could predict high digital wellness. Practical implications Educational Institutions should combine their AI-literacy training with digital wellbeing programmes instead of conducting them independently, focus on instilling self-efficacy and self-regulation over peer norm messages, and treat AI-literacy training as a wellbeing intervention in addition to an academic skills intervention. Originality/value This paper shifts the focus of AI literacy from its association with digital usage to digital disengagement and presents a methodologically triangulated (PLS-SEM, ANN, fsQCA) explanation for how competency, awareness, and affect influence the Generation Z intention to engage less with harmful digital practices.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is entering psychotherapy at almost every point of clinical work: therapist training, screening and detection, risk prediction, diagnostic support and treatment planning, patient education, chatbot-delivered session content, between-session tracking, supervision, and documentation. Discussion of the associated dangers to this process has so far been overwhelmingly patient directed. This narrative review addresses these questions from a futures-oriented perspective: what AI may do to psychotherapists as professionals. We first map current and emerging applications across the phases of therapy. We then distinguish four forms of competence loss reported in the wider clinical literature, namely deskilling, never-skilling, mis-skilling, and moral deskilling, and use them to structure a function-by-function analysis of nine clinical tasks. The risks we identify, most of which rest on extrapolation from medicine and education and are therefore best read as hypotheses, extend beyond technical skill. Algorithmic flags may redistribute clinical attention, and accountability may shift from the quality of judgement to adherence to procedure. Case formulation may close prematurely, and theoretical pluralism may narrow toward the traditions best represented in training data. Findings that chatbots are rated as more empathic than clinicians may threaten professional identity, while supervision may lose its relational and formative functions. We then set out four possible trajectories for the field: AI as a support to professional judgement, gradual dependency, standardized AI-mediated practice, and systems designed explicitly to preserve and cultivate expertise, together with the drivers that may lead toward each. Implications are drawn for training, clinical governance, and professional ethics.

items.abstract_text: Disruptions in the supply chain (SC) are occurring more often and becoming more complex, posing significant challenges for engineering management and operational resilience. Current prediction methods do not adequately reflect the relationships and uncertainty among variables, as well as the causal factors of disruption events. In this study, we present a novel uncertainty-aware hybrid framework, namely, the University of Queensland Creative Arts/Creativity Network (UQ-CRGATNet), which introduces Dynamic Graph Attention Networks (DGAT), a tab transformer network for contextual feature learning, resilience-aware representation, Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, and an ensemble meta-learner of Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Categorical Boosting (CatBoost). Moreover, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Non-combinatorial Optimization via Trace Exponential and Augmented lagRangian for Structure learning (NOTEARS) enable feature attribution and causal disruption analytics that are human-understandable and support trustworthy decisions. The proposed framework is a joint model that models graph-structured relationships, heterogeneous tabular information, predictive uncertainty, and resilience indicators within a unified learning architecture. The extensive experiments performed on a real-world supply chain dataset show that they significantly outperform conventional machine learning, ensemble learning, and transformer baselines. UQ-CRGATNet achieves excellent Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) and Precision-Recall characteristics, with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 99.87, 99.87, 99.89, 99.88, and 99.73%, respectively. The uncertainty-guided ensemble will increase prediction accuracy, while causal analytics will provide actionable managerial insights into the drivers of disruptions. The results show that the proposed framework provides a strong, interpretable, and scalable solution for proactively predicting supply chain disruptions and supporting resilient engineering management.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into diverse fields, including education, where it offers innovative approaches to enhance self-regulated learning (SRL). For many students in Chinese higher education, developing robust SRL skills remains a significant challenge. This review addresses the need for a clearer understanding of how AI tools influence these skills by synthesizing ten empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following the PRISMA framework, the literature was identified from prominent academic databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC. Drawing on Zimmerman’s SRL Three‑phase Model, this synthesis suggests that AI tools show potential to assist students with goal‑setting and foster motivation within the forethought phase. During the performance phase, such tools may support learning‑strategy deployment and progress monitoring via timely feedback. In the reflection phase, AI can facilitate outcome evaluation and subsequent strategy adjustment. However, the review also identifies potential risks, such as student over-reliance on AI, and notes a limited research focus on long-term SRL development and group regulation. Accordingly, future research should adopt longitudinal designs, investigate AI’s role in co-regulated learning, and integrate AI literacy and emotional support into SRL development frameworks. items.title: Classification AI vs Generative AI in grading and feedback

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Marking is among the most time-consuming activities in education, and artificial intelligence (AI) is widely proposed as a remedy. Attention has centred on generative large language models, yet regulators raise concerns about their bias, consistency, and explainability. This paper contrasts generative grading with per-question classification models trained only on an educator’s own marking and deployed in a human-in-the-loop workflow. The architectures are compared against criteria drawn from regulatory guidance: transparency, construct-relevant features, determinism, and specifiable training data. A narrower role for generative models is also identified, in composing and restructuring marker-approved feedback rather than in marking. Deployment analytics from one platform are then reported, covering approximately 166,000 marked questions, 39,500 essays, and six institutions: 66.2% of questions were marked in under one minute, 77.6% to 89.5% of AI suggestions were accepted, and essay models reached a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.93 for high-confidence predictions. Questionnaire responses from earlier pilots (33 markers, 30 students) are also reported: markers described marking as faster and consistent feedback as easier to provide; most students rated feedback more consistent and higher in quality. Implications for institutions selecting or building such tools are discussed, alongside the limitations of vendor-collected data.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence can provide explanations and comments on circuit solutions, but its educational value depends on how students interpret and use those responses. This focused narrative review examines the use of generative AI to help students identify and correct errors in introductory circuit analysis. Published sources were identified through OpenAlex searches, publisher records, and reference checking, with full-text assessment informing selection and synthesis. Twelve reports were selected for their relevance to circuit reasoning, feedback, or learner verification; an electronics-course perception study provides an explicitly adjacent comparison. Foundational research on formative feedback and self-regulated learning informs the interpretation. The synthesis addresses circuit representation and diagnostic accuracy, students' use of feedback, and the interpretation of educational outcomes. Technical evaluations show that input representation, reference information, and computational support shape the conditions under which responses are assessed. Classroom and tutoring reports describe opportunities for explanation, comparison, revision, and instructor intervention. The selected reports provide more direct evidence of perceived usefulness than of independently retained understanding. Observational grade associations and a historical-cohort comparison offer additional perspectives, although their designs limit causal interpretation. The review proposes teaching considerations that preserve students' initial reasoning, check the represented circuit, focus guidance on a specific difficulty, and require students to justify corrections. These considerations are derived from the literature and have not been evaluated as a combined intervention. The principal implication is that AI feedback should be judged through the accuracy of its diagnosis and the student's subsequent reasoning. Selective coverage, heterogeneous outcomes, and AI-assisted selection and extraction constrain the review's conclusions.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread throughout the world and is used, knowingly and unknowingly, because of the speed of its services. People live under an illusion about AI’s advancement, which creates profound barriers to human security in the digital world, harms people in the real world and creates risks to fundamental human rights. In response to this risk, the European Union has adopted a significant regulatory model, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). The Act prohibits several AI practices, such as manipulation, and provides risk-based protection so that AI systems are transparent and accountable to people and governments. As a result, AI systems can be reconciled with human safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. However, incidents of AI manipulation have occurred, including the violation of a child’s right to life, and many other incidents are taking place, especially affecting vulnerable AI users, because many countries lack binding legal protection. Legislation on AI is not limited to technological innovation but also concerns human security, transparency and accountability. Bangladesh produced the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2024 (NAIP) and later the National AI Policy 2026–2030 (Draft v2.0), which provides some important protections for human lives against AI manipulation, including data protection and cybersecurity, grounded in Bangladeshi culture. However, the policy focuses on public services, innovation and economic growth, primarily to fulfil the technological ambitions of Vision 2041 in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Consequently, human security and protection from AI remain an option rather than a primary goal among the policy’s commitments. Not only Bangladesh but most South Asian countries lack protection for people, especially the vulnerable, against AI manipulation. This qualitative legal research therefore examines the adequacy of AI governance and enforcement in Bangladesh in protecting digital security and fundamental rights. Drawing comparative insights from the EU AI Act, it examines gaps in Bangladesh’s digital legislation and institutional practice and identifies best practices. It also compares practice in the neighbouring countries of India and Pakistan to assess Bangladesh’s position within South Asia’s regional AI governance framework. Through a critical analysis of primary and secondary sources, it finds that Bangladesh and its neighbours have adopted policies but lack adequate protections and binding laws to govern AI systems, leaving people living blindfolded.

items.abstract_text: Background With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated strong potential to transform healthcare research and practice. However, LLMs are probabilistic and generate inherently variable outputs, which create risk and uncertainty in healthcare applications. Therefore, analyzing the current research landscape of ChatGPT applications is imperative to understand applied techniques and related concerns and to facilitate their practical integration into healthcare information systems. Objective Leveraging LLM-based agentic AI with domain experts to analyze trends in ChatGPT healthcare applications and to examine the collaborative and interpretative capacities of LLM agents in broader contexts beyond narrowly defined topics. Methods The review used a systematic search of the PubMed and Web of Science databases, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and focused on ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors. To support the review process, an adaptive, iterative LLM-based agentic AI with a human-in-the-loop mechanism was employed for automated metadata extraction, identification, classification, and knowledge synthesis. The extracted information was subsequently used for temporal and thematic analyses, citation network construction, and main-path analysis. Results Across 192 papers, the review identified 511 ChatGPT application types, 690 concern items, and 368 influence usage factors distinct from traditional IT, achieving a metadata error rate of 1.04%. The human-agentic AI workflow enabled efficient synthesis of contextual information across studies, addressing the growing challenge of timely evidence integration in medical knowledge. The findings provide insights into the evolving trajectories of ChatGPT applications in healthcare and demonstrate the value of an expert-validated human-agentic AI workflow in supporting literature analysis and streamlining review processes. Conclusion This review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors in healthcare. The study further provides meaningful insights into the operational mechanisms of agentic AI, demonstrating the potential of human–AI collaboration for medical informatics research.

items.abstract_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune condition associated with markedly elevated cardiovascular disease (CVD) morbidity and mortality. Both disproportionately affect women and racial and ethnic minority populations, highlighting the profound influence of social determinants of health (SDOH) on disease trajectories. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on socioeconomic determinants and lifestyle factors that contribute to CVD among individuals with SLE and evaluates emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in CVD risk prediction and management. A comprehensive search (PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science; 2012–2026) identified original research, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and guidelines reporting CVD-related outcomes in SLE. Evidence demonstrates strong associations between low socioeconomic status, limited healthcare access, and educational inequities with heightened CVD risk. Black, Hispanic, and Latin American individuals experience disproportionate CVD burden due to intersecting structural, social, and clinical barriers. Modifiable lifestyle factors, including physical inactivity, tobacco use, and suboptimal dietary patterns, further exacerbate risk. Emerging ML-based studies suggest improved individualized CVD risk stratification in SLE compared with traditional general-population risk calculators, highlighting the potential for precision-focused approaches. Equity-centered strategies integrating clinical care with SDOH are essential. AI-enabled tools offer promising avenues for personalized risk prediction and resource optimization; however, rigorous attention to algorithmic fairness, transparency, and health equity is essential to ensure responsible implementation. This is the first review to synthesize SDOH, lifestyle factors, and AI in an equity-centered SLE-CVD framework, given AI’s rapid expansion in rheumatology and the urgency of addressing cardiovascular health inequities in SLE.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly emerged as a promising resource for supporting students with dyslexia. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature examines AI primarily as an assistive technology, with limited attention to the cognitive mechanisms through which it may enhance reading development. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework that integrates Baddeley’s multicomponent model of working memory with contemporary AI-supported educational tools. Drawing on research in cognitive psychology, special education, cognitive load theory, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and self-determination theory, the paper argues that AI should be understood not merely as an instructional aid but as an external cognitive support system that complements and extends the functional capacity of working memory during reading. Specifically, the framework illustrates how AI technologies—including text-to-speech systems, speech recognition, adaptive learning environments, and generative AI applications—may reduce cognitive load while supporting the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, and episodic buffer. Through this cognitive alignment, AI has the potential to facilitate decoding, comprehension, learner engagement, and reading autonomy among students with dyslexia. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded perspective that connects cognitive theory with emerging educational technologies. Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of a specific intervention, the paper provides an integrative model to guide future empirical research, instructional design, and the development of AI-supported reading interventions for learners with dyslexia.

items.title: Navigating Digital Distractions: A Phenomenological Study of Students’ Lived Experiences in Technology- Rich Learning Environments
items.venue: International Journal of Research on Multidisciplinary Studies

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Digital devices support learning but can also divert students’ attention, and little is known about how students experience this in technology-rich classrooms in Bukidnon, Philippines. This qualitative study used a descriptive phenomenological design to explore the lived experiences of Grade 12 Humanities and Social Sciences students with digital distractions at Bocboc National High School during school year 2026–2027. Fifteen students were purposively selected and interviewed individually using a researcher-made, semi-structured interview guide. The interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed, and the transcripts were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged. In interrupted flow, learning was broken by digital pulls and followed by guilt, anxiety, and embarrassment. In a layered pull against focus, distraction arose from habit and platform design, peer pressure, fatigue, and home and school conditions such as shared devices, weak connectivity, and unclear device rules. In reclaiming control, students removed tempting sources, structured their time, set boundaries with others, and drew on personal motivation. In shared responsibility, students called on teachers, parents, peers, and the school for clear rules, engaging teaching, and support. Two accounts differed from the rest, attributing distraction to lesson quality and to limited access, respectively. Learning in a technology-rich environment therefore appeared as a continuous negotiation between digital temptation and academic purpose. The study addresses a gap in Philippine phenomenological research, which has centered on the Visayas and Davao, by describing student experiences in an inland province of Northern Mindanao. Supporting focused learning may require student self-management together with consistent device policies, purposeful instruction, and stable, equitable access to connectivity. Future studies may include other schools, compare urban and upland settings, and add teachers’ and parents’ perspectives.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly gained attention as a tool to support teachers in lesson planning, yet pre-service teachers often lack the knowledge and prompting skills necessary to integrate it effectively into their practice. This study employed a formative research design to investigate how pre-service teachers used GenAI for lesson plan development through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework and to identify instructional guidance that fosters more meaningful interactions. Across two semesters in an introductory educational technology course at a large US university, 137 pre-service teachers engaged in lesson planning activities with GenAI tools. Data sources included student-AI chatlogs, reflective blog journals, and instructors’ reflective notes. items.title: Manipulation without Lies: AI Hyperpersuasion and the Limits of the Deception Paradigm

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

items.abstract_text: Large language models can now outperform human persuaders in controlled settings, and they do so in whichever direction they are instructed to persuade. Regulatory and ethical responses to this development nevertheless remain anchored in what this article calls the deception paradigm: the assumption that communicative influence becomes wrongful when, and because, it involves false assertion. The article argues that this paradigm systematically fails to capture AI hyperpersuasion. Drawing on the philosophical literature on manipulation, it shows that hyperpersuasion characteristically operates through true but selectively curated content, adaptive framing, simulated intimacy, and the exploitation of individually diagnosed cognitive dispositions – techniques that bypass rather than deceive rational agency. It then examines Article 5(1)(a)–(b) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Although the prohibition is conceptually open to manipulation without deception, its operative test – material distortion, appreciable impairment of informed decision-making, counterfactual decision change, and significant harm – is inherited from unfair commercial practices law and reproduces the architecture of fraud, leaving paradigmatic cases of hyperpersuasion untouched. Extending the analysis from individual autonomy to democratic epistemology, the article contends that hyperpersuasion threatens democracy not primarily by aggregating individual harms but by degrading the epistemic conditions – independence of judgment formation, a shared space of reasons, and the contestability of public claims – on which collective self-government depends. Regulating hyperpersuasion therefore requires a shift from content-based tests of falsity and harm to process- and relationship-based criteria that target asymmetric epistemic power.

items.abstract_text: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into mental health support settings, understanding how individuals engage with AI‐based tools for psychological support is increasingly important. This study introduces the nine‐item AI‐Assisted Psychological Support Use Scale (AAPSU), a behavioural measure of how people use conversational or generative AI for emotional regulation, self‐reflection, well‐being‐related decision‐making and support‐seeking. The scale development process included item generation, expert review, pilot testing, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and reliability testing. EFA identified two theoretically coherent subscales: self‐regulatory and reflective use (six items) and substitutive use (three items). CFA provided internal confirmation of this structure, with satisfactory model fit and strong factor loadings. Convergent‐validity analyses showed meaningful associations with attachment to AI systems, attitudes towards AI in mental health contexts and AI mindset. These findings support the AAPSU as a brief, reliable and theoretically grounded measure of AI‐assisted psychological support use while indicating the need for replication in more diverse samples.

items.abstract_text: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

items.abstract_text: The rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed organizational practices by providing new opportunities to improve employee productivity, work efficiency, and professional performance. This study examined the influence of Generative AI adoption on employee performance in digital finance and marketing organizations in Pakistan, focusing on the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technostress. These findings emphasize that technological integration alone may not ensure improved organizational outcomes unless employees are adequately supported in adapting to AI-based working environments. The study further highlights the importance of providing AI-related training, improving digital competencies, and developing supportive workplace policies to minimize technostress. From a theoretical perspective, the research contributes to understanding the combined influence of technological adoption and employee psychological factors on workplace performance. The findings offer practical guidance for commercial banks, FinTech institutions, and digital marketing organizations in developing employee-centered AI adoption strategies that promote work engagement, reduce technological stress, and strengthen overall organizational productivity.

Despite increased scholarly attention in organizational studies (OS), research on AI integration remains fragmented, lacking robust theoretical frameworks that address its unique characteristics. This study addresses this gap by systematically mapping the theories applied to AI research within OS and critically evaluating the extent to which these frameworks reflect AI’s unique characteristics in organizational contexts. Second, we critically assessed the utility, falsifiability, assumptions, and boundaries of these theories in addressing AI’s distinct characteristics in organizational settings. Our evaluation of the theoretical landscape highlights the importance of critically assessing the boundaries of borrowing, blending, or constructing theories and the need for more integrated theoretical models that encompass both the technological-performance and relational-human dimensions of AI. Based on our findings, we provide guidelines for organizational scholars to evaluate and develop robust theories, advancing the theorization of AI research in OS.

items.abstract_text: Nigeria’s mental health system serves less than 10% of those in need, with severe provider shortages and deep-seated stigma. Generative AI chatbots offer scalable support, yet how Nigerian adults experience attachment to non-human therapeutic agents remains unexplored. To examine lived experiences of AI therapeutic relationships among Nigerian adults, focusing on attachment formation, cultural acceptability, and perceived authenticity within contexts of care scarcity. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis with 37 adults (18–45 years) who engaged AI mental health chatbots for ≥ 4 weeks. Semi-structured interviews explored relational experiences, trust development, privacy concerns, and comparisons with human/traditional healing. Four superordinate themes emerged: (1) Relational Ambivalence ; participants valued 24/7 availability and non-judgmental space yet struggled with perceived lack of genuine human reciprocity; (2) Cultural Navigation ; users actively adapted Western therapeutic frameworks to local idioms of distress, blending AI interactions with family counsel and spiritual practices; (3) Stigma Sanctuary ; chatbots provided confidential entry points circumventing community visibility and professional hierarchy; and (4) Fragile Dependency ; prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about potential app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human escalation pathways. Most participants maintained “instrumental intimacy”; emotional reliance tempered by awareness of algorithmic artifice. Nigerian adults develop pragmatic, contextually mediated attachments to AI therapeutic agents that reflect both global digital therapeutic trends and local specificities of care scarcity, stigma, and pluralistic healing. AI chatbots function not as human substitutes but as bridging objects temporary relational anchors in systems of profound unmet need. Findings suggest ethical deployment in LMICs requires culturally adaptive design, transparent algorithmic boundaries, and mandatory human handoff protocols to prevent dependency in unsupported contexts. items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND: In recent years, there has been a notable surge in the ability of machines to perform complex and intelligent human-centered tasks, particularly within the domain of cardiovascular health. Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms reflect the considerable potential for such analyses to meaningfully extend into translational device development and clinical usage of medical devices, especially mechanical circulatory support (MCS) therapies. Here, we investigate and report the applications, limitations, and strategies in which AI is currently being employed in MCS and the potential opportunities of AI approaches to advance the field of MCS. METHODS: To effectively assess the scope and impact of AI in MCS, we conducted a systematic literature review. A comprehensive search of 4 recognized research databases (PubMed, Google Scholar, Ovid MEDLINE, and ProQuest) was performed using this Boolean string: "(Artificial Intelligence) AND (AI) AND (Mechanical Circulatory Support) AND (MCS) NOT (Heart Transplant) NOT (Cardiogenic Shock) NOT (Critical Care)." This strategy was designed to identify the application of AI in MCS only. Database search results were then screened by titles and abstracts, followed by full-text eligibility assessment and duplicate removal. Following these screening and eligibility steps, 30 of the 328 identified articles remained for inclusion. RESULTS: Most relevant publications covered two main subjects: the prediction and management of postoperative outcomes, and the development of personalized device-patient matching and timing. Across the reviewed studies, AI/ML models demonstrated promising performance in study-specific predictions of complications, recovery-related outcomes, and survival and were investigated as tools to support clinical decision-making. Barriers to broad implementation of AI include the necessity for sizable, high-quality datasets to achieve algorithm training benchmarks, the lack of organized and complete databases, such as INTERMACS, and limited computational resources. Emerging frontiers of MCS recognize the potential for AI and ML techniques to refine image recognition capabilities, diagnostic assessment, device placement, and post-implantation monitoring approaches in the future. CONCLUSIONS: AI-driven approaches demonstrate a promising convergence of computational power and clinical expertise, with the potential to support more personalized, efficient, and informed management of MCS patients. However, the current evidence remains largely exploratory, and broad implementation will require robust clinical validation together with attention to data integrity, model accuracy, resource access, and clinical acceptance.
